entries.title: The Senate Passes Its College Sports Bill, Setting Up a House Fight
entries.summary: The bill passed 77-22 after a more than five-year battle over regulating college sports.
entries.content:
The NCAA and conferences scored a huge win in the Senate on Monday after spending more than five years — and a whole lot of money — pushing Congress to regulate college sports.

The Protect College Sports Act passed 77-22, immediately moving the focus to whether it can pass the House next. Democrats. Sens. Two Republicans, 19 Democrats and Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, voted against the bill. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Maria Cantwell (D-Washington) were the lead co-sponsors of a bill that would provide the NCAA and conferences antitrust protection to set rules for athlete compensation, eligibility and the transfer portal.

Proponents say that legal shield is necessary to rein in the free spending of the name, image and likeness, or NIL, era, during which athletes are receiving over-the-table money from schools for the first time. The bill’s loudest opponents, however, say it’s an unfair check on athlete earning power, particularly in the high-revenue sports of football and men’s basketball.

But the PCSA also deals with far more than compensation, even if those sections have naturally stirred the most public debate. The bill permits schools to explore pooling their television rights to sell as a massive package in the future, amending the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961. It also attempts to limit further conference realignment, among many other regulations. Because of how sprawling the bill is, lobbyists and aides predict a complicated path in the House, which is not scheduled to be in session again until after the midterms.

The bill has faced pushback from major labor organizations, the Congressional Black Caucus and a few Senate Democrats. Sens. Chris Murphy of Connecticut and Cory Booker of New Jersey, two of the main opponents to the bill, have framed the PCSA as a labor and civil rights issue, arguing that athletes should have a real say in any negotiations over congressional legislation. But the bill reached at least 70 yeses in every vote in the Senate, signaling that a handful of Democrats were willing to break with the labor community — most notably the AFL-CIO — to support a bill backed by President Donald Trump.

The PCSA has four Democratic co-sponsors in the Senate: Cantwell, Chris Coons of Delaware, Peter Welch of Vermont and John Hickenlooper of Colorado. On the Republican side, Cruz was joined by Sens. Eric Schmitt of Missouri, who was key to pushing the bill through the Senate, and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and John Hoeven of North Dakota.

The late blitz of amendments, including a vote for seven of them Monday night, perhaps previewed the fights to come in the House.

The Senate adopted an amendment from Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisconsin) for athletes to retain the right to sue in state court over abuse, fraud and safety failures. It then adopted an amendment from Sen. Tim Scott (R-South Carolina) that would require schools to disclose to Congress any money received from foreign governments, state-owned companies or sovereign wealth funds for athletics.

And then, by voice vote, the Senate agreed to an amendment from Sens. Ashley Moody (R-Florida) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut) to raise the maximum number of teams in a power conference from 19 to 20.

Not adopted? An amendment from Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana), a vocal critic of the PCSA, that would have capped ticket prices. An amendment from Booker to raise a catastrophic injury fund from $100 million to $200 million. (It needed 51 votes and received 50). Plus another amendment from Booker to restrict pay and job movement for coaches much like the PCSA would for athletes. That failed 52-47.

Last week, Booker and Murphy filed an amendment to cap coaches' salaries at $5 a million a year, a way to highlight their view that athletes are being shortchanged by the PCSA. And for much of the last month, Moody has pushed for tweaks to how the PCSA would regulate future conference realignment, pulling a number of Florida politicians into her effort. Moody would like to see schools such as Florida State and Miami have the flexibility to switch leagues in the near future if the opportunity arises.

“For every Ashley Moody in the Senate, there are five in the House, if not more,” a Republican House aide told The Washington Sun. “There are going to be a lot of opinions on this thing.”

Some aides are expecting the House to rehash key issues from the SCORE Act, a Republican-backed bill that tried (and failed) to regulate college sports in 2025. Unlike the PCSA, the SCORE Act explicitly said college athletes could not be classified as employees, something Republican House members could raise again, according to multiple aides.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise suggested this summer that the issue could derail the bill, telling Politico: “For the House to be able to take anything up, you got to prevent employment status of the student athletes.”

Two Republicans — Sen. Jon Husted of Ohio and Rep. Tim Walberg of Michigan — recently introduced a bill that would prohibit college teams from offering more than 20% of their roster spots to international athletes. That could make international athletes another pet topic for some Republicans as lobbying shifts to the House.

On the other side of the aisle, Democrats have typically stayed in lockstep with the CBC when it comes to college sports, though the Senate votes raise the question of whether some might peel off to support the PCSA.

All of this, though, is only relevant if the House gives the PCSA the time of day. Cruz has told multiple reporters that the House could return before the midterms to take up the bill, though there’s skepticism in the House that will happen. If it doesn’t, the bill could still be a lame duck item in the House, a complicated process in itself. A tall hurdle was cleared Monday, especially since no college sports bill had even reached a full Senate or House floor vote in recent years. But many still remain.

This story has been updated to include the final vote breakdown.

entries.title: Second Lawsuit Filed Against Trump’s Birthright Citizenship Rules
entries.summary: The class-action suit challenges Trump’s newest executive order seeking to strip citizenship from children of certain classes of parents.
entries.content:
A group of immigrant parents filed a class-action lawsuit against President Donald Trump on Monday, arguing that his latest attempt to uproot birthright citizenship violates the 14th Amendment and more than a century of Supreme Court precedent.

The case, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., centers around Trump’s August executive order, which aims to strip citizenship from children born in the United States via surrogacy, to a parent employed by international organizations or to a parent the government claims to be a gang member.

“For Plaintiffs — children who will be denied citizenship under [the order], and their parents — and for families across the country, [the order] seeks to strip away the ‘priceless treasure’ of citizenship, threatening them with a lifetime of exclusion from society and fear of deportation from the only country they have ever known,” the legal complaint states.

A federal judge in Marylandalready blocked the new order from being enforced against children covered by an earlier class-action suit, calling it “almost certainly unconstitutional” as applied to that group. Monday’s lawsuit seeks protection for a broader class of families targeted by the new restrictions, including some who fall outside the earlier case’s parental immigration-status requirements.

Before that, the high court ruled against the president in Trump v. Barbara, striking down his Day 1 executive order seeking to end birthright citizenship for children born in the U.S. to undocumented parents.

The Monday filing, made by attorneys for the American Civil Liberties Union and other advocacy groups, focuses on three families named as plaintiffs in the class-action suit. The plaintiffs contend the restrictions unlawfully expand narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship, including one for children of foreign diplomats with full diplomatic immunity.

One child, referred to as “Nathan” in the filing, was born in Washington just days after Trump’s second executive order. Nathan’s mother is French-born and has spent ten years in D.C. Both parents work for international organizations and hold visas for that type of work, according to the complaint.

Another plaintiff, an Australian father identified as “Edward,” is expecting a child through a U.S. surrogate in October. His eldest daughter, also born through surrogacy in the United States in 2021, is an American citizen.

The complaint also challenges new documentation requirements that attorneys say could burden families beyond those directly targeted by the order. State Department guidance calls for sworn “attestations” from both noncitizen parents seeking a child’s passport, a requirement the plaintiffs argue could be impossible to meet when a father is unknown or unavailable.

Those attestations will be “difficult or even impossible to provide,” the complaint states, effectively denying proof of citizenship to “people even beyond those targeted” by the executive order.

Affected children could face denial of passports and Social Security numbers, barriers to benefits and the threat of deportation, the lawsuit alleges.

Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, highlighted the group’s previous successes in a press statement Monday announcing the new lawsuit.

“The Constitution is clear, and the Supreme Court has been clear: Birthright citizenship is the law of the land,” Wofsy said. “The Trump administration’s newest attack on this fundamental American principle is just as cruel and illegal as its previous executive order, and it will meet the same fate in court.”

The White House did not immediately respond to The Washington Sun’s request for comment.

entries.title: Hegseth Says National Security and Military Cyber Forces Will Guard U.S. Election
entries.summary: The announcement comes after President Donald Trump gutted the civilian agency specifically created to safeguard election infrastructure.
entries.content:
By Jonathan J. Cooper

The U.S. National Security Agency and other military intelligence and cybersecurity forces will guard election systems during the November midterms, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Monday.

Military cybersecurity experts have routinely helped monitor systems and deter potential hackers since election equipment was designated “ critical infrastructure ” in 2017.

But Hegseth's announcement comes after President Donald Trump gutted the civilian agency specifically created to safeguard election infrastructure, a division of the Department of Homeland Security called the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. That agency last week released an election infrastructure security plan that lays out potential threats to election systems and lists services it would offer to election officials to protect the vote.

Both announcements come just weeks before Election Day on Nov. 3 and with early voting already underway. The short timeline “suggests this is just theater,” said David Becker, a former U.S. Justice Department attorney who leads the nonprofit Center for Election Innovation & Research.

“If the administration was serious about assisting state and local election officials, they shouldn’t have dismantled all of the federal government’s election cybersecurity capacity and fired all their experts in early 2025,” he said.

Though cybersecurity assistance from the NSA and U.S. Cyber Command is routine, many elections experts, civil rights groups and Democratic election officials are on guard for signs of meddling in voting or ballot counting by the Trump administration. The president continues to push false claims that elections are rife with fraud while trying to interfere with longstanding election procedures.

The U.S. Supreme Court blocked an attempt by Trump to restrict mail voting but has allowed the use of a federal database to check the citizenship of voters.

In a memo dated Sept. 22 and publicly announced Monday, Hegseth directed defense intelligence officials to mobilize every resource “to defend our election infrastructure from foreign malign influence and ensure that every lawful voter can cast their ballot free from foreign intimidation, coercion, or fear.”

___

Associated Press writer Nicholas Riccardi in Denver contributed to this report.

entries.title: What $750,000 Buys You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia
entries.summary: Our weekly column compares listings across the DMV.
entries.content:
While fall is a time of renewed energy in the D.C. area, as school and sports kick into high gear, the housing market is doing the opposite: fading and drifting like autumn leaves. The most recent stats from Bright MLS show that the August slowdown is likely to continue into the fall, particularly as mortgage rates remain elevated.

But the good news for those ready to buy: There’s more choice. Listings of homes for sale were up 11% last month compared to August 2025, in part because some homes are staying on the market longer. That gives buyers some negotiating room.

We thought we’d see what buyers can get in the District, Maryland and Virginia for around $750,000. Keep in mind that taxes are different in each location, so they’ll need to be calculated with an agent or lender.

Which one would you choose? Or, have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming column? Let us know at metro@washingtonsun.com.

 

D.C.

Untitled
The listing: 608 Kenyon St. NW

The price: $750,000

The specifics: This three-bedroom, four-bathroom townhouse with just under 2,100 square feet was built in 1912. It’s less than a mile from the Columbia Heights Metro station.

The vibe: City living with a house hacking option.

What makes it special: This property includes a legal one-bedroom apartment that can be rented out to help offset the mortgage. The last tenant paid more than $1,600 per month for the apartment, according to the listing. The area, on the home’s lower level, could also be used for additional living space. The townhouse has a two-car garage, a prized feature for urban living. The main level has an updated kitchen with stainless steel appliances and granite counters, an office, a half bath and access to the private backyard. Upstairs are two bedrooms and two full bathrooms. The whole house has hardwood floors.

Agent: Mark Hudson, Corcoran McEnearney


Maryland

Untitled
The listing: 5408 Marlin St., Rockville

The price: $749,900

The specifics: This five-bedroom, three-bathroom single-family home, which has almost 3,200 square feet, was built in 1967 and extensively updated in recent years.

The vibe: Updated traditional suburban with walkability.

What makes it special: This split-level house, which has four levels, sits on one-third of an acre and is walking distance from a shopping center plus the middle school and high school. The owners refinished the hardwood floors and replaced the roof, siding and electrical panel. With five bedrooms, there’s plenty of room for larger households or guests, plus space for entertaining in the family room, which has a fireplace and a beamed ceiling. The eat-in kitchen has a breakfast area with a brick wall and bay window, and the dining room has sliding glass doors to the newly refinished deck and backyard.

Agent: Jane Weissman, Coldwell Banker Realty

 

Virginia

Untitled
The listing: 339 Piedmont Ave., Washington

The price: $724,000

The specifics: This five-bedroom, three-bathroom home has 3,252 square feet on a one-acre lot. Built in 2002, this ranch-style home was recently updated with new siding, new trim, a new deck and a new patio.

The vibe: Country village chic.

What makes it special: If you’re looking for a taste of upscale small-town life about 70 miles from downtown D.C., this home in Washington, Virginia, (known to locals as “Little Washington”) offers convenience and privacy. Residents can walk to shops, galleries and restaurants in town, including the renowned Inn at Little Washington, or entertain in their own backyard. Inside, multiple bedrooms provide space for guests or family members. The house has been updated with wide-plank bamboo flooring, new doors, custom shelving, newly tiled bathrooms and designer lighting, including chandeliers in many rooms.

entries.title: New Database Tracks the Education Outcomes of D.C. Students
entries.summary: The dashboard tracks wage, career, higher education and equity information for former students of D.C. schools.
entries.content:
What happens after graduation for students of D.C.’s schools? What about students who don’t graduate? On Monday, the Office of the Deputy Mayor for Education and the Office of Education Through Employment Pathways (ETEP) launched an interactive dashboard that offers a first of its kind look into those questions and others exploring the economic mobility of the District’s students.

Through 10 briefs, users can peer into median income based on education attainment, the employment rate of grads and the industries D.C. alumni work in. Administration and support positions top the list for all students, but health care comes first for those who go beyond a bachelor’s degree.

“This cross-agency view helps us understand how pre-K-12 education, higher education and workforce programs shape access to families sustaining careers,” ETEP IT Director Seth Shapiro said. “Our work provides actionable insights for program providers, policymakers, agency leaders, educators and the public.”

The data shows that former students who attain more than a high school diploma earn around $20,000 more than those with just a high school degree, which Shapiro believes demonstrates that higher sectors of education “reliably pays off” in rising-wage industries.

However, he notes the majority of former D.C. students are concentrated in “flat-wage industries,” which tend to have less opportunity for growth. Former D.C. students who have post-baccalaureate degrees have a median annual income of nearly $54,000 — closest to the D.C. living wage of $55,000.

“While wages do increase to higher levels with higher levels of education, many local learners still do not reach the living wage threshold,” Shapiro said. “By visualizing the gap, we can better identify where additional supports and interventions may be needed.”

The data is not an exhaustive list of the potential economic mobility of all D.C. students. The data includes the class of 2016 and students enrolled after that time, and employment data includes information only for alumni working in D.C., not including federal workers. Currently, datasets include only public and charter school students.

The datasets are being used to inform D.C.’s Compact for 2043 initiative, which by 2043 seeks to have a 90% graduation rate and for 100% of students to have a post-graduation plan across all District public schools. DCPS’ graduation rate was just under 78% for the 2024-2025 academic year.

Relevant data collected by ETEP will also be used by D.C., Maryland and Virginia’s multi-state Student Pathway Report, which in its first phase is tracking student movements and outcomes across the capital region.

A total of seven agencies worked in the development of the software. Community stakeholders, including members of the all-parent governing board, Parents Amplifying Voices in Education (PAVE), had a say in the dashboard’s scope. They expect the database to grow as more information becomes available.

“We see our education system as a reflection of all of us as a community, and we believe data shines the spotlight on how we can better love our most precious members, our children,” PAVE founder Maya Martin Cadogan said. “Data is key to understanding what is and isn't working, and when done well, data helps all of us set aside our biases to work together.”

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: ‘Redeemed Again’
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Sept. 29, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: A mistrial for Trayon White, Lime-assisted crime and what to make of the Nationals’ season.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 8/10. More peeks of sunshine and pleasantly warmer temperatures give the digit a nice boost. Full forecast from Capital Weather.

THE LATEST

By Monday morning, federal judge Rudolph Contreras had seen enough: He declared a mistrial in the Trayon White bribery case, The Washington Sun’s Jenny Gathright reports.

The jury remained deadlocked, and continued discussions had only cemented their divergent positions on whether to convict White, jurors wrote in a note to the court.

White was accused of pocketing tens of thousands of dollars of illegal bribes from a D.C. contractor, who acted as an FBI informant and allowed authorities to secretly film his meetings with the council member. Videos of the meetings showed White accepting envelopes of cash and discussing plans to use his position to steer grants toward his associate’s companies.

But to convict White, the jury had to find that he not only accepted the money, but also intended to carry out a bribery scheme. White’s defense argued that the lawmaker never planned to follow through on his promises to the contractor.

U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro said her office would retry the case.

White, speaking to reporters on Monday, said he felt “redeemed again” and thanked God, his supporters — and even his enemies — for keeping him motivated through one of the hardest periods of his life. When asked by a reporter what he accepted the money for, White deflected and said he wanted to focus on his job as a D.C. Council member.

“Let’s stick to the topic,” he said. “We want to accept the jury’s decision today, regroup and get back to work.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

The Getaway Car Scooter. Lime is cracking down on misuse of its e-bikes and scooters, which police say are being used to flee crime scenes, The Sun’s Zara Norman reports. The company collaborates with D.C. police to track down suspects if issued a subpoena or warrant, and plans to restrict underage or unsafe use of its vehicles as part of a $17 million investment in D.C.-based initiatives. It already slowed maximum speeds and introduced facial-scan age verification … but it clearly hasn’t deterred every malfeasant scooter-rider.

D.C. Has a New Tool to Track Student Outcomes. Yesterday, the Office of Education Through Employment Pathways (ETEP) released a first-of-its-kind look into the economic mobility of the District’s students, The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports. Users can get insight into wage, career, higher education and equity information for former students of D.C. schools. The data has some limitations. It doesn’t include students who may have moved to other states and federal workers are not included on the dashboard.

Some DMV parents are seeking “vaccine-optional” pediatricians who will treat their children regardless of vaccination status, Axios D.C. reports.

D.C.’s presumptive next mayor, Janeese Lewis George, is striking a careful diplomatic balance in the months before she’s likely to take office. In a Q&A with Washingtonian magazine, she reiterated her willingness to work with a broad coalition — including, when appropriate, the Trump administration — on the city’s economic challenges, while simultaneously vowing to “stand up to anyone” who threatens the District’s local autonomy.






FROM VIRGINIA

Dulles International Airport’s center runway has been closed for planned maintenance and infrastructure improvements through November, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports. Communities north, south and west of the airport will experience more flight traffic until the project is completed.

Trips to Virginia’s motor vehicle offices may not take all day anymore. Wait times have plummeted to a record-low average of 8.3 minutes — down from 37 minutes in 2019 — after sweeping operational reforms that also saved the agency $15 million, the Virginia Mercury reports.





FROM MARYLAND

More than 40 rabbis are calling on Montgomery County’s Public School district to take action against what they say is an alarming rise in antisemitism among students, The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports. According to Bethesda magazine, a teacher reported a swastika carved into a desk to administrators at Walter Johnson High School. MCPS saw a nearly 137% increase in hate-bias incidents in its system last school year, which it attributes to better training. The rabbis’ letter asks MCPS to adopt more “substantive teacher training and experiential teaching programs, along with more consistently [enforced] social media guidelines.”





WHAT YOU GET FOR $750,000

32-new_004.jpg (5999x3999, AR: 1.50)
This week’s real estate column looks at what buyers can get for around $750,000 across the region.

Where is this house listed? Click on your guess to see the answer:

  1. Maryland
  2. Virginia
  3. D.C.
We’ll let you know tomorrow how many of you got it right.






SPORTS

Was the Nationals’ 2026 season, which came to a close Sunday, a success or a failure? That’s a nearly impossible question to answer, writes The Sun’s Jesse Dougherty, who takes note of both the big steps the franchise has taken under Paul Toboni, the Nats’ first-year president of baseball operations, and the fact that fans are rightfully running out of patience.

“The farm system, I think for the most part there have been a bunch of great strides there,” Toboni said. “But I think like most things in this game, that’s pretty fragile and doesn’t necessarily mean that those strides are going to continue into the future if we don’t really stay on it.”

The Sun’s Alex Schiffer and Dave Sheinin were in attendance for the Wizards’ Media Day on Monday, including an entertaining interview session with star guard Trae Young, who didn’t seem particularly concerned over having played in just five games for Washington a season ago. “I’m actually very grateful for what happened last year because if we didn’t, we don’t necessarily have AJ Dybantsa,” he said of the team landing the No. 1 pick in the draft.

entries.title: Morning Sun: Believing the Polls
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Talking about the polls with pollsters. A scoop about chaos at the IRS. Senate Republicans punt Trump’s Pentagon reconciliation request. How battleground Democrats talk about trans rights now. And: A follow-up to our scoop from last year about Lindsey Halligan’s security detail. 

Editor’s note: We goofed! Some of you received our Metro newsletter by mistake yesterday. But if you liked what you saw, you can sign up here.





THE LATEST

We’re doing that polling thing again. “First of all, the polls are fake,” Donald Trump told reporters at the White House yesterday when asked about the myriad surveys showing his party’s candidates struggling in red places like Iowa. (Polling errors in Iowa near the end of a closely watched national election? Impossible!)

In the D.C. universe, this midterm has entered foregone-conclusion land. The question on everyone’s minds is now, how much do Democrats win by? Many think the answer is, at least, a lot. Why is everyone so sure? The polls! The same things everyone was looking at in 2024 when Trump beat the prognosticators, in 2025 when Democrats in New Jersey beat the prognosticators and throughout 2026 when primary voters confounded the prognosticators on a regular basis.

Pollsters say: We got this. “I think that there were some total overreactions to polling relative to some of the primary results,” Matt Taglia, senior director at Emerson College Polling, told The Washington Sun’s Manuela Silva. “There are always going to be instances where the margin is off, but polling primaries is a lot harder than polling general elections.”

People who do polling do not just say stuff. They try very sincerely to back it up. “There’s nothing that we’ve seen in the polling that is positive for Republicans,” Taglia said. He is not the only pollster saying this. Basically every pollster is saying this. Hence the confidence in the numbers.

But numbers that say what, exactly? “People tend to look at the overall bad numbers for Trump and the economy and think that automatically carries over to big Democratic margins or big Democratic gains relative to 2024,” Charles Franklin, who runs polling for Marquette Law School in Wisconsin, told Manuela. “I think there’s plenty of evidence that these toss-up seven or eight Senate races sure look like toss-ups.”

Could Democrat James Talarico break the mold and win a Senate seat in Texas? Polls say: Sure! Could Republican Ken Paxton do what Republicans always do in Texas and win? Quite easily! That’s literally what the polling says. Same story in many Senate seats across the country.

“Everybody needs to get off their high horse,” says Crystal Ball’s Larry Sabato, who puts together election predictions from a long list of detailed factors. “It’s interesting, and you know I retweet a lot of the polls, you know, because people are interested in that. But it’s not gospel. It is not handed down by Moses … The numbers can be wrong.”

But even those on the bad side of the polls say they can’t argue with the bottom line. “I don’t think people believe polling fully because they’ve been so wrong so often,” a MAGA operative told The Sun’s Jasmine Wright, “but I think the vibes, if you just take a good look at that, don’t look good.”

  • Alito bows out of blockbuster Supreme Court climate case (Politico)




FROM THE IRS


Scoop: Everyday they’re reshufflin’: Leadership at the IRS tried to reassign around 1,500 employees with no relevant experience to help process tax returns. But that effort failed, The Sun’s Eric Katz reports. Now, staff are being reassigned again, this time to a new internal consulting office. Several workers impacted by the changes told The Sun that staff are being moved to new teams without any indication of what work they will perform.

The changes have been orchestrated by Joe Ziegler, the official the Trump administration promoted after he alleged to Congress the IRS had mishandled Hunter Biden’s taxes. Eric has stories from inside the IRS about a workforce that is beleaguered and nervous amidst the ongoing chaos.

FROM THE HILL


Pentagon funding request punted: The White House is hoping to push through a $350 billion additional package for the Defense Department through reconciliation. But Republicans remain divided over how to finance the buildup, The Sun’s Joe Gould reports, and there is no immediate path for the reconciliation package before the recess.

More: Susan Collins Says Challenges to Trump’s Latest Spending Cuts Are Coming

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


Democrats got comfortable moving right on trans messaging: Democratic candidates are pushing back on versions of Trump’s famous/infamous “they/them” ad with their own ads touting their votes to “to keep transgender ideology out of our schools,” as an ad for Rep. Marcy Kaptur in Ohio put it. “I think you’ve seen a willingness from some of the groups, when in the past you might not have seen it as much, to give people in the red states more space and grace to have these conversations. Even if it’s not 100% the ideal ACLU position on trans issues,” a Democratic strategist told The Sun.

The Sun’s Alex Roarty and Oriana González take a deep dive into these politics, and find Democratic candidates using more anti-trans language. Despite what that strategist said, there are still plenty in the party wary of this shift: “It is simply unacceptable to use the Republican framing that ‘boys should not play in girls’ sports’ because you’re calling trans girls ‘boys.’ It’s deeply disrespectful and it’s actively harmful,” a House Democrat told The Sun.

First on The Sun: Democrats barn dance in NC’s 11th. Hurricane Helene remains a defining issue in western North Carolina two years after the storm ravaged the mountainous region. Fresh off a recent race rating move to “toss up” by the Cook Political Report, Democrats are focusing on their nominee Jamie Ager’s local ties with a new six-figure buy featuring a spot filmed at his monthly “mountain hoedowns,” our Christa Dutton reports. In the spot, Ager tells viewers, “I’ll fight for our Helene recovery funds.”  

More: Drunk Driving Incident Roils the Wisconsin Governor’s Race





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Follow-up: Lindsey Halligan’s million-dollar detail. During her four months as a White House-appointed federal prosecutor last year, the Department of Justice spent $1.1 million on an unusually large security detail for Halligan, The Sun’s Jose Pagliery and Derek Hawkins report. Last year, Jose was first to reveal the phalanx of U.S. Marshals that shadowed Halligan at all times. “They follow her around the building, even in our office on the various floors. Insane waste of money,” a source told The Sun at the time.

entries.title: Republicans' Trans Attack Ads Aren’t Hitting the Same Way This Year
entries.summary: A potent 2024 message risks falling flat, with Democrats adjusting and the economy overpowering.
entries.content:
Republicans in tight races are trying to rekindle some old magic: hammering Democrats on transgender policy and praying a message that worked so well in the 2024 election can save them this November.

The problem is that even if their attack is the same, a whole lot else has changed.

In short, the public’s perception of each party on transgender issues has shifted. Republicans’ former economic subtext is no longer helpful, and — perhaps most significantly — the Democratic response has undergone an overhaul, with some candidates and incumbents adopting anti-trans rhetoric in key races. Taken together, it’s created a radically different backdrop for the deluge of anti-trans attacks — one that threatens to undermine their effectiveness.

“There's been a sea change over the past two years,” said Lanae Erickson, the senior vice president for social policy, education and politics for the moderate Democratic group Third Way. “And there's a lot more space for Democrats to be able to say things out loud than they could have two years ago, without backlash.”

Democrats, by their own admission, were caught flat-footed on trans issues in 2024. And many party strategists say the issue still has enough resonance with voters that Democratic candidates can’t simply ignore the attacks.

But even conservative groups are warning that the GOP’s focus on transgender issues isn’t landing with voters the same way it did in 2024, when the attacks were often paired with a positive economic message.

The conservative American Principles Project, which has pushed Republicans to use anti-trans messaging, said in a memo released earlier this month that Republicans could not solely rely on trans issues to win elections: “Pressing the advantage on these issues alone, while important, may not be sufficient.”

APP president Terry Schilling told The Washington Sun that the memo is not meant to deter Republicans from using anti-trans messaging. “This is like the one area where the Republicans have a clear contrast to go on offense.”

The problem, Schilling said, is that Republicans don’t have an economic pitch to pair with their culture message.

“Here's where we're weakest: Voters are still hung up about $5 a gallon gas, about the war in Iran,” Schilling said.

Voters now favor Democrats when it comes to handling the economy, according to some polls. That’s a turnaround from 2024, when the public’s favorable view of Trump’s economic agenda was crucial to his election.

Even the party’s most well-known ad on trans issues in the last election — a spot that accused then-Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris of being for “they/them” instead of the average American voter — also touted Trump’s plan to cut taxes for the middle class.

But the economic portion of the argument has been lost this year.

“They missed too much of the rest of the ad,” said one Republican strategist involved in Trump’s 2024 campaign, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “The rest of the ad was about that President Trump is going to fight like hell to turn around the economy.”

The party’s use of so many ads that focus on trans issues instead of the economy, the strategist added, risks making it look as if the GOP is the party fixated on the trans community instead of the day-to-day cost of living.

“We appear to have misplaced priorities because we are leaning into issues that voters don’t think about every day,” they said.

A Fox News poll released in April found that 56% of Americans now say Democrats do a better job when it comes to transgender issues, compared to 43% who said they thought Republicans do. And a June poll by the LGBTQ advocacy group GLAAD found that 65% of registered voters “believe politicians are often using transgender issues as a distraction from more important priorities.”

Republicans are trying to defend slim majorities in the House and Senate this year in what even Republicans acknowledge is a challenging political climate. Democrats have tried to boost their chances by distancing themselves from some of the party’s most unpopular positions in 2024, including on transgender policy.

Lindsay James, who’s running for a House seat in Iowa, said in an ad: “We need common sense rules to keep sports fair for boys and for girls,” while Josh Turek, the Democratic Senate candidate in Iowa and a former paralympian, told The New York Times, “I don’t believe that biological males should compete against females in sports.”
trans_ads_midterms.jpg (814x453, AR: 1.80)In Ohio, the Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton told The Toledo Blade, “I do not support boys in girls’ sports.” And the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas, James Talarico, told Fox News that he opposed “trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness,” and that he would “absolutely” vote for a bill to ban gender-affirming surgeries for minors. (These types of surgeries are rarely performed on minors.)

Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown has run his own response ad belittling Republicans’ focus on trans issues. And Sarah Trone-Garriott, a House candidate in Iowa, has explicitly rebutted other Democrats in her own ads.

“I approve this message because politicians have become too extreme on these issues, and I'll always put kids and families first,” Trone-Garriott says in one ad.

A Democratic strategist, granted anonymity to speak candidly, told The Sun the breakthrough for Democrats using more anti-trans language came last year, when Rob Sand, now the Democratic nominee for governor in Iowa, was asked by a conservative radio host whether he thought transgender girls belonged in girls’ sports. Sand responded with a simple “no.” The strategist said the moment immediately circulated among party political strategists.

“Rob Sand just did it, and it was fine,” the strategist said. “There’s power in numbers, and all you have to do is tell these people that you have the majority opinion. And then you can just say it.”

Democratic strategists have said the party has broadly concluded that the issue is enough of a concern to voters that candidates can’t ignore it, especially in red states and districts. They also say the larger Democratic ecosystem has given candidates more space to talk about the issue without as much backlash from local and state LGBTQ advocates, Democratic allies and even campaign staffers.

“All of these guys are operating with empathy and sympathy for the trans community and understand they must be protected from discrimination and violence,” the second strategist said.

But, the strategist added, “they have to talk honestly about difficult questions. And I think you’ve seen a willingness from some of the groups, when in the past you might not have seen it as much, to give people in the red states more space and grace to have these conversations. Even if it’s not 100% the ideal ACLU position on trans issues.”

When The Washington Sun asked the American Civil Liberties Union to respond to this quote, the organization did not condemn candidates who have taken a turn on trans issues in their campaigns.

“The ACLU is a nonpartisan organization that does not endorse candidates for office. We do believe in — and the research supports‚ an approach that allows pro-equality candidates to communicate clearly to voters in a way that upholds their principles while neither sacrificing trans people's dignity nor losing sight of the core economic issues far more likely to decide their electoral fate," said Kris Hayashi, the group’s campaign director for transgender rights, in a statement.

The party’s approach has not been uniform: While some have reiterated their support for trans people, other lawmakers have broken with the caucus and voted in favor of anti-trans legislation. Trans activists and families with trans children have condemned Democrats for distancing themselves from the community.

Still, the party has continued to have conversations around how it can best address these issues this cycle.

In April, the centrist New Democrat Coalition invited Third Way and tThe Trevor Project, an LGBTQ youth advocacy group, to advise House Democrats on how to address trans issues, according to two sources familiar with the matter and one House Democrat who attended the session.

“Everyone has been crystal clear that it is simply unacceptable to use the Republican framing that ‘boys should not play in girls’ sports’ because you’re calling trans girls ‘boys.’ It’s deeply disrespectful and it’s actively harmful,” the House Democrat told The Washington Sun.

That’s why, the House Democrat said, Democrats have been “blindsided” by ads like Ohio Rep. Marcy Kaptur’s.

“Here’s the truth: I voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools because parents know what’s best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls’ sports,” Kaptur, who is in one of the most competitive House races in the country, said in one ad.

The ad was denounced by the Lucas County Stonewall Democrats, a local LGBTQ group, which said that Kaptur is “against the LGBTQIA+ community.” Though there was no mention that Kaptur’s record says otherwise: She voted against Republicans and in favor of trans athletes being able to participate in female sports just last year.

But Democrats in Republican-leaning districts are under pressure to respond. One Democratic strategist estimated that fully half of the GOP’s messaging this year has been around transgender issues — about the same time they’ve given the economy, data centers, immigration and crime put together.

Democrats involved in efforts to combat the GOP’s trans message say they’re hopeful that their strategy is already working — and if so, the issue won’t be so prevalent in future races.

“I hope we never have an election cycle like this again,” Third Way’s Erickson said.

entries.title: The IRS Is Reshuffling Staff Without Telling Them Why
entries.summary: The tax agency tried to turn more than a thousand HR and IT staffers into tax processors. That failed. Now they’re being assigned to a team that remains a mystery.
entries.content:
When the IRS reassigned around 1,500 employees with no relevant experience to help process tax returns, the agency said the moves would help provide “the best possible experience for taxpayers.”

Months later, after extensive training and failed exams, the IRS is abandoning the efforts.

The employees will now be transferred again, this time to a new internal consulting office. Joe Ziegler, the official the Trump administration promoted after he alleged to Congress the IRS had mishandled Hunter Biden’s taxes, is behind the new job assignments.

Ziegler spearheaded the first round of employee reshuffling, which sent IT and human resources staff into the Taxpayer Services office. After giving up on that idea — few employees were ever actually processing returns and none did so during peak tax season — Ziegler is placing the staff onto new teams without any indication of what work they will perform, according to several workers impacted by the changes.

The whipsaw has sparked fear and panic among IRS staff. It also shows the remarkable responsibility placed in an untested leader as the agency continues to reshape itself after pushing out tens of thousands of employees.

In another unusual twist, senior executives the IRS sidelined in early 2025 and kept on paid leave for nearly a year and a half have been called back to lead these consulting teams. The agency recalled the executives to work in recent weeks without explaining to them why they were pushed out or suddenly called back.

“Nothing has been assigned yet,” one impacted worker who requested anonymity because of their current employment said. “People are asking questions, but no one is being given answers.” The IRS employee added that management is “just doing whatever they want and forcing people to fight it.”

The agency placed around 50 career IT executives on leave in March 2025, causing speculation that the IRS was trying to ease information sharing with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Only a handful of those executives will return to help lead the new teams; many others have accepted settlement agreements to leave the government.

IRS has assigned employees to one of three divisions within the internal consulting office, with one formerly sidelined senior executive leading each. What functions those divisions will carry out remains a mystery. The fraction of reassigned employees who passed their certification exams were also provided an option to voluntarily remain in their Taxpayer Services role.

Employees have pushed leadership for more details on their fate, though at least one supervisor has told them they would need to submit a Freedom of Information Act request to receive it. Some of those FOIA requests have already been denied, one employee said.

The roughly 1,000 originally reassigned IT employees are prohibited from returning to their old roles, according to employees and internal communications viewed by The Washington Sun. Some have expressed concern the agency will eventually lay them off.

Most of the roughly 500 HR employees who were reassigned have returned to the human capital office.

For now, Ziegler is telling the former IT staff only that the new assignments will boost agency consistency. He told employees he was implementing a Reporting and Organizational Correction that will “allow us to operate with a single, authoritative source of organizational truth.”

The IRS has shed around 25,000 employees — about a quarter of its workforce — since President Donald Trump took office, mostly by offering incentives for staff to leave. More than 8,000 of the departed employees worked in processing tax returns, providing customer service by phone or in person, or in other roles directly related to filing season. The agency had hoped the reassignments would help stabilize its most public-facing operations in the wake of those cuts.

Before abandoning the effort, officials had suggested to employees the tax processing assignments would last as long as it took to bring down backlogs that had been in place for years. A large percentage of the employees never passed the necessary certification exams to conduct the work, however.

Around 150 employees originally reassigned to tax processing have spent extended time being paid not to work —some for more than a year — according to employees and internal emails. Those workers will now join the new teams with to-be-determined roles. In messages to that group, leadership had taken to referring to those employees as “outcasts.”

Some of those employees saw the new assignment as a step in a positive direction.

“I’m just glad to have something to do,” one staffer said.

entries.title: D.C. Is Seeing the Rise of a New Kind of Getaway Vehicle: E-Scooters
entries.summary: Lime has denounced the use of its electric scooters and bikes to help suspects flee the scene in recent crimes.
entries.content:
D.C. continues to struggle in cracking down on the use of a getaway car for the modern age: Lime scooters, which police say have recently been used by criminals fleeing the scene in a spate of crimes including shootings, an attempted robbery and a fatal stabbing.

That the ubiquitous lime-green, electric bikes and scooters were able to be used in crimes — with suspects still at-large — has raised questions. Lime requires users to verify their age with facial scans before each ride, and asks for government ID if there’s room for doubt.

Last year, the company slowed maximum speeds in an effort to curb the problem. And while the company doesn’t just hand over its user data, if D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Department produces a warrant or subpoena, Lime has a dedicated law enforcement team that works with police to assist in investigations, a spokesperson told The Washington Sun. The company recently helped police track down suspects in both London and Chicago.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“We do not tolerate the use of our vehicles to commit crimes and stand prepared to support MPD in any investigation into these alleged incidents,” Erika Duthely, Lime’s regional head of government relations, told The Sun. “Would-be criminals in D.C. should understand that if they use a GPS-tracked Lime vehicle to break the law, MPD can subpoena this information in their investigations.”

A spokesperson for MPD said it “works closely with all private businesses in the district to keep our community safe,” exploring “every avenue that may assist in identifying and apprehending suspects in criminal cases.”

In some instances, MPD has shared that suspects fleeing on Lime’s scooters were under the age of 18. Lime restricts use of its scooters to adults, and this spring rolled out an AI feature that performs facial recognition scans before each ride. Thousands of rides, a Lime spokesperson said, have been blocked due to suspected underage riding since then.

Clearly, plenty of kids are still figuring out how to skirt the rules.

“We’ve spent much of 2026 working to better prevent underage riding and to crack down on anyone allowing underage riding on their accounts,” Duthely said.

The company continues to try and tackle the problem, and a spokesperson pointed out that misuse of its vehicles accounts for a small fraction of the 4.5 million rides D.C. residents have embarked on.

This fall, the company is rolling out another feature in D.C.: using sensors on e-scooters to identify “prohibited riding behavior, including burnouts, jumps, and skidding,” according to a press release. Repeated behavior like that will result in fines, account suspensions or expulsion from the app.

It’s part of a wider investment Lime is making in the city: The company recently announced that it has invested more than $17 million in D.C. initiatives, which includes refreshing its fleet of 8,000 vehicles.

“We’re intent on serving Washington D.C. for years to come and we will continue to emphasize equitable access to our vehicles, aim to deliver the highest standard of operational excellence, encourage safe riding and proper parking, provide top-of-the-line hardware and technology, and sustain a robust team equipped to serve the nation’s capital,” Lime CEO Wayne Ting said in a press release.

entries.title: Senate Republicans Are Leaving Trump’s $350 Billion Defense Boost in Limbo
entries.summary: “We have to just make the case to every single Republican and as many Democrats as will listen,” said Sen. Kevin Cramer.
entries.content:
Senate Republicans are preparing to depart Washington at the end of the week without approving President Donald Trump’s request for $350 billion in defense funds, leaving the Pentagon to confront how much of its ambitious spending plan can fit into the regular budget.

Lawmakers, Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg and other senior Pentagon officials held multiple closed-door meetings over the past two weeks about the department’s overall $1.5 trillion budget plan. But Republicans remain divided over how to finance the buildup, and there is no immediate path for the reconciliation package before the recess, which ends Nov. 9.

The administration has split its defense ambitions among three funding tracks: a regular budget of roughly $1.15 trillion, roughly $350 billion through the Republican-only reconciliation process and a separate $67 billion supplemental spending request to cover unbudgeted costs from the Iran war. Trump said in his address to the United Nations last week that he wants a total defense budget of $1.5 trillion.

Senate defense hawks are on board. But deficit-minded Republicans are unwilling to add hundreds of billions of dollars in defense spending without cuts elsewhere to offset them. Democrats — who usually supply at least some votes for national security spending — are reluctant to help fund an Iran war that polls show is unpopular with voters.

Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi), the Senate Armed Services Committee chair, said he believed there was still time for the Senate to craft its own package before the recess begins this week.

But Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wisconsin), whose support as Senate Budget Committee chair would be crucial to moving a Republican-only package, said he had no plans to do so until after November’s midterm elections.

Johnson said Feinberg and other Pentagon officials he met with this month made a compelling case for the added spending, but the offsets he would need have not been identified.

“We have to satisfy the deficit hawks like we satisfy the defense hawks,” he said. Asked what that would require, he said, “Pay for it.”

Senate defense hawks are pushing for a reconciliation package that exceeds $300 billion and includes the president’s Golden Dome missile defense shield, munitions replenishment and production-line expansion, and at least some portion of the administration’s supplemental request.

“We have to just make the case to every single Republican and as many Democrats as will listen, and even if it comes down to a 50-senator vote, we need to socialize and keep pushing the importance of this,” said Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee. “Defending the country is the most legitimate, and in some respects, the only legitimate thing the federal government does.”

Cramer, whose state is expected to play a role in Golden Dome, panned the House-passed reconciliation instructions, which set aside only $60 billion for the Pentagon. He wants the Pentagon to get the entire $350 billion.

Identifying $350 billion in cuts to offset that spending would be a daunting task, both politically and budgetarily. The figure amounts to one-fifth of discretionary spending proposed for 2027, while much of the rest of the federal budget is tied up in mandatory programs such as Social Security and Medicare, or interest on the debt.

Pentagon officials have already been mulling what happens if Congress does not provide all of the defense plus-up through reconciliation.

Pentagon Comptroller Jay Hurst said this month that Congress was working to incorporate some Pentagon priorities into the discretionary spending bill if the administration does not get everything it wants through reconciliation. He specifically pointed to the munitions investments Feinberg has championed.

If approved, that spending would underpin the administration’s push to sharply expand weapons production, including a long-term production ramp-up for missile interceptors, Tomahawk missiles and more. The Pentagon has reached several framework agreements with weapons makers, but they depend on Congress providing the money.

Moving those priorities into the regular budget wouldn’t necessarily solve the Pentagon’s problem. The appropriations process is also stalled. Congress is funding the government at current levels through Dec. 11, leaving major decisions for the lame-duck session, when lawmakers return after the midterms with a clearer sense of each party’s leverage heading into the next Congress.

“Last year we got 11 and a half of the [appropriations] bills done, and I hope that we could get them all done, but you never know,” said Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), the Senate Appropriations Committee chair. “That depends on whether the Democrats are going to cooperate.”

Even before Congress resolves those larger funding questions, the Pentagon is already reshuffling money among existing accounts to cover immediate operational demands, including costs associated with the Iran war.

The department has deferred maintenance and some training to manage shortfalls while facing higher-than-expected personnel costs — and the Navy has said it is $6 billion to $8 billion short just to cover Iran war costs.

The Pentagon has asked Congress to let it shift $4.3 billion in existing funds, including $3.76 billion for higher-than-expected personnel costs, drawing money from shipbuilding, aircraft procurement and research and development.

“Their options get narrower and narrower as you get closer to these accounts running out of money,” said Rep. Rob Wittman (R-Virginia), the vice chair of the House Armed Services Committee. “Many of the places they’ve been able to go to get these dollars are running very thin now.”

There has been an “uptick” in Pentagon reprogramming requests, which allow the department to shift money Congress approved, from one account to another, according to Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, the top Democrat on the Senate defense appropriations subcommittee.

Coons said that as he considers those requests, he has had to balance his opposition to Trump’s war with Iran and making sure that troops in the fight might run out of money, citing problems with the USS Abraham Lincoln’s extended deployment.

“I'm conscious that there is the possibility that if they are not able to reprogram some funding, you've got both Army and Navy units deployed that could run into shortfalls operationally,” Coons said. “I don't want another USS Lincoln situation where you've got a lack of fuel and food.”

Hurst disputed the idea that the Pentagon is making substantially more or more urgent reprogramming requests than usual. Still, he acknowledged, “The kinds of things we’re programming might be a little different than normal.”

If the extra money never materializes, some of the Pentagon’s plans could just take longer. Byron Callan, a Wall Street analyst at Capital Alpha Partners, expects some of the spending envisioned for reconciliation to be spread across defense budgets over the next five to eight years.

Key Democrats, such as Sen. Jack Reed of Rhode Island, say the uncertainty along all three funding tracks makes it more important that the Pentagon realistically identify its top priorities for Congress.

“What they have to do is put in a budget bill what they absolutely need,” said Reed, an appropriator and the ranking member on the Senate Armed Services Committee. “That will require them to compress their spending in some areas and expand in areas like munitions. We need to see a coherent plan, not three different initiatives.”

entries.title: Betnijah Laney-Hamilton Is Right at Home With the WNBA’s Youngest Team
entries.summary: The Mystics’ midseason addition brings valuable playoff experience to a roster that has almost none.
entries.content:
Michaela Onyenwere was thrilled when the Mystics brought in Betnijah Laney-Hamilton.

Back when Onyenwere was a rookie, playing for the New York Liberty in 2021, Laney-Hamilton had been her favorite vet. “She was somebody who was consistent every single day, not only in her work ethic, but also just in her accountability,” Onyenwere said. “I was like, OK, that’s somebody I can really look up to.” She was naturally excited to reunite as teammates when the Mystics claimed Laney-Hamilton off waivers in August. The acquisition meant that the team would be getting both valuable depth on the wing and valuable leadership in the locker room, Onyenwere thought.

And one more thing.

The acquisition meant that Onyenwere would no longer be the oldest player on the Mystics.

On the youngest team in the WNBA, loaded with rookies, Onyenwere sometimes feels like a senior citizen. “They always joke about how old I am,” she sighs, at the ripe age of … 27. The Mystics’ youth is clear in everything from their dancing to their social media to their team nickname. (They’ve taken to calling themselves the “Young Hos” — good luck printing that on a rally towel.)

It has made for a delightful romp of a season as the team has outperformed projections and cruised into the playoffs. But as they prepared for their stretch run, they decided they could use a bit of a veteran presence, and they found that in 32-year-old Laney-Hamilton.

“We’re super energetic, and we’re excited for everything, but I think she keeps us stable and focused,” said Mystics reserve guard Lucy Olsen. “She’s been really great for us.”

And they have been great for her.

“To sum it up,” Laney-Hamilton said, “it’s just been fun.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

As the fifth-seeded Mystics have entered the playoffs — dropping Game 1 against the No. 4 Dream on Sunday, with a must-win Game 2 scheduled for Wednesday — her leadership has been key.

Few players in the WNBA can match her breadth of experience. Laney-Hamilton played for five franchises in her first seven years in the league — battling for minutes and bouncing from team to team in search of a steady role. As she was starting to gain her footing, she tore her ACL, sidelining her for a full season. Then, after those difficult early years, Laney-Hamilton broke through. She won the league award for Most Improved Player in 2020 after notching 17.2 points and 4.0 assists per game with the Dream. That performance cleared the way for her stint with the Liberty, where she became a key piece of the organization, eventually starting every playoff game of a championship run in 2024.

But the years since have been challenging. Laney-Hamilton tore her meniscus last spring and missed the entire season that followed. Working her way back from the injury this year, she did not find consistent minutes under new Liberty coach Chris DeMarco. Trade rumors abounded. She was ultimately waived. It led her to the Mystics, where she has found joy in becoming the resident vet.

“It’s a lot of youthful energy,” said Laney-Hamilton, who turns 33 in October. “It keeps things lighthearted, while at the same time being very competitive, very serious about what we do. I think that shows both on and off the court. Just how fun we are, the way that we celebrate each other, the way that we encourage each other, and then the way that we go out there and compete.”

Her career trajectory means that she can relate to everyone on the roster. Laney-Hamilton knows what it’s like to be a playoff starter and what it’s like to be on the end of the bench and everything in between. “It’s great to have her knowledge,” said Mystics rookie forward Cotie McMahon. “Just so much IQ.”

Laney-Hamilton has worked off the bench since joining the team, averaging 4.2 points in 15.5 minutes per game, a very different role from what she had a few years ago. This group has quickly embraced her as a leader all the same.

“To see her integrated into our team that quickly and that seamlessly has been really cool,” said Onyenwere. “She’s been a sounding board for us. She’s a voice for us. … She brings things that are intangible.”

Her playoff experience is especially valuable. The majority of this group had never been near the postseason before this year; the rest of the roster had a combined two career playoff starts before Game 1. Laney-Hamilton had 25. The coaching staff has leaned on her even more over the past week.

“She’s talking from a position of authority, credibility. She’s been there, done that,” said Mystics coach Sydney Johnson. “It can really give our players an added level of confidence.”

Yet for all the emphasis on her wisdom and experience and veteran status, Laney-Hamilton has still very much clicked with this group as just another player.

“She's older, but she's so young-minded and spirited,” Olsen said. “She fits right in.”

Which leaves just one question: Is there an age limit on being a Young Ho?

“Honestly, yes, and she is past that limit,” said McMahon, one of the chief architects of the nickname. “But she’s still considered a Young Ho.”

entries.title: Lone Republican Senator Derails a Bill to Prevent Demolition of the Kennedy Center
entries.summary: Sen. Mike Lee blocked a bill that would have prohibited the demolition of any national memorial honoring a U.S. president.
entries.content:
Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prohibited the destruction of any national memorial honoring a U.S. president — a measure meant to protect the Kennedy Center from a full demolition — without congressional approval.

The proposed bill, led by Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Oregon) and Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), comes after President Donald Trump threatened to have the performing arts facility “ripped down” if he does not receive explicit recognition for the more than $250 million renovation project for the center.

The senators attempted to pass the Protecting Presidential Memorials Act Monday evening through a process known as unanimous consent — a procedure that allows legislation to bypass typical Senate rules unless a lawmaker objects. The one-page bill would have blocked any potential demolition of the Kennedy Center, Lincoln Memorial and Thomas Jefferson Memorial, memorials that pay homage to U.S. presidents, without an act of Congress.

But Lee objected to the bill’s passage when Merkley brought it to the floor.

“Unfortunately, a colleague objected to this common-sense bill,” Merkley said in a statement released Monday. “Trump’s threats are straight out of the authoritarian playbook and should infuriate every American who values our nation’s history and the rule of law.”

Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island), Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) and Jack Reed (D-Rhode Island) also co-sponsored the legislation.

“Democrats should join us in lowering the cost of living and securing American elections instead of wasting the Senate’s time with partisan scaremongering they haven’t even tried to run through the appropriate committee process,” Lee wrote in a statement to The Washington Sun about his objection.

The morning after Lee blocked the bill, Merkley and Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine) introduced it in both the House and Senate.

“For Donald Trump to attempt to usurp this great memorial by putting his own name above JFK’s — and then threaten to demolish the building if he doesn’t get his way — is beyond the pale,” Pingree said in a press release. “When Congress designates a place to memorialize a president, no administration should be able to tear it down on a whim. This bill establishes a simple safeguard: if Congress created the designation, only an act of Congress can authorize its demolition.”

Trump has unwaveringly pursued a more than $250 million renovation project for the center that he has claimed is in a “virtual state of collapse,” despite mounting concerns from lawmakers and the public about shuttering the iconic D.C. landmark for two years. The performing arts center has been closed since Sept. 15, and a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to give the court 30 days’ notice before moving forward with any demolition project.

The president has taken specific issue with the court blocking the addition of his name, in various capacities, to the front facade of the building.

In a 71-page brief filed Monday, the Justice Department — which is representing Trump in his ongoing legal battle over the center — argued that the Kennedy Center Board of Trustees' previous votes to affix Trump’s name to the building had been struck down in “error.”

“Further, the recognition of the President’s contributions does not constitute a ‘memorial’ as that word is ordinarily understood in this context, and thus the statutory prohibition does not apply,”

DOJ attorney Brett Shumate argued. “Instead, it merely serves to acknowledge the Trump Administration’s, and President Trump’s, present and future efforts to renovate and restore the Center. Such acknowledgements of major donors are common at similar facilities, and

Congress did not prohibit such a sensible recognition here.”

Shumate also asserted the center has become “dangerously dilapidated” and “fundamentally unsafe to employees and patrons alike,” and Trump’s efforts are the “sole hope for the Center’s financial survival and structural renewal.”

entries.title: Media Outlets Urge a Judge to Keep Blocking Trump's White House Ban
entries.summary: CNN, MS NOW and Politico say the White House has continued to “unpredictably and inconsistently” implement Trump’s policy even after a federal judge temporarily blocked it.
entries.content:
CNN, MS NOW and Politico urged a federal judge on Monday to extend his order blocking President Donald Trump from banning their journalists from the White House grounds.

Judge Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee in Washington, D.C., issued a temporary restraining order Thursday blocking the ban and restoring access to the media outlets. But the news companies now are seeking a preliminary injunction that will last until the case is over, asserting that the Trump administration has continued to improperly restrict their coverage.

“The White House has persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban, including by barring CNN from fulfilling its role as designated television network pooler on September 26 — to the detriment of CNN, its fellow pool members and, ultimately, the American public,” the filing says.

In the filing, Theodore J. Boutrous Jr., who represents the news companies, urged Kelly to extend his order before it expires. The “irreparable harm Plaintiffs have already suffered from the ban will quickly compound” if the president is allowed to restrict their access to the White House once again, the filing says.

The media outlets repeatedly contended in court that the ban violated their First Amendment and due process rights. Kelly found in his order that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their due process claims because the White House confiscated media passes without giving the journalists prior notice or the opportunity to be heard, but he did not address the First Amendment concerns levied by the outlets.

“The President and his administration have continued to make clear that this ban has only one purpose: to punish reporting he doesn’t like,” Boutrous said in a written statement released with the filing. “That’s retaliation and viewpoint discrimination, pure and simple.”

entries.title: Americans Are Growing More Pessimistic About the Economy
entries.summary: Prices for gas and other items remain elevated.
entries.content:
By Matt Ott

Americans’ confidence in the economy sank to the lowest level in more than a decade this month as prices remain elevated and wages stagnate amid the ongoing Iran war.

The Conference Board said Tuesday that its consumer confidence index tumbled 6.7 points to 81.9 in September, down from 88.6 in August. That’s the lowest reading in the board's survey since April 2014 and below the lowest level reached during the pandemic.

Respondents’ views of their present situation fell by 7.9 points to 109.3. Their short-term outlook also slid, falling 5.9 points to 63.6.

Americans remain flustered by the economy after five years of elevated inflation, potentially posing a risk to President Donald Trump and Republicans in the midterm elections, which are a little more than a month away.

Write-in responses to the board’s survey, collected from September 1-23, were mostly pessimistic this month, with frequent references to the high cost of gas, goods and services.

“The Consumer Confidence Index deteriorated notably in September, following two prior months of softening,” said Dana Peterson, the Conference Board’s chief economist, adding that consumers’ views of current business conditions became negative for the first time since September 2024.

Trump has continued to blame high prices on his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden, yet inflation has risen since Trump’s inauguration last year.

Earlier this month, the government reported that consumer inflation accelerated last month and gas prices spiked as fighting in the Middle East dragged on. The consumer price index rose 3.4% last month compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Friday, just like July. But inflation quickened month to month as costs jumped 0.4% from July, quadrupling the 0.1% registered in the previous month.

The Federal Reserve two weeks ago raised its benchmark interest rate for the first time since 2023 in an effort to quell stubbornly high inflation, and the central bank signaled another rate hike could occur later this year.

The quarter-point increase lifted the Fed’s key rate to about 3.9% and, over time, could result in higher borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and credit cards.

Gasoline prices — which currently average $4.46 for a gallon of regular — are not all that is rising. Prices for appliances, car repairs, and wireless phone services also jumped in August.

The most recent measure of the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge — the personal consumption expenditures price index — was up 3.7% in June from a year earlier. That was down from May’s 4.1% year-over-year increase but up from 2.8% before the Iran war began on Feb. 28. It was 2.5% when Trump was inaugurated in January 2025.

The government issues its August PCE data Wednesday.

Consumers’ views of the current labor market also worsened in September, but remained in positive territory, the board said. Respondents broadly said they expected their household incomes to rise, but not as much as in previous months.

The U.S. labor market bounced back in August as employers added a surprising 162,000 jobs, ending a summer of lackluster hiring. The unemployment rate remained at a low 4.1%, but some of that can be attributed to significant numbers of people giving up on their search for employment in previous months.

Inflation has dominated conversations this year in business and households, and meager pay raises have made rising prices more painful for many. Average hourly wages rose 3.1% last month from a year earlier, the weakest year-over-year increase since May 2021.

The government issues its September jobs report on Friday.
