entries.title: U.S. Ban on $1 Billion Worth of Canadian Imports is Now in Effect
entries.summary: The ban includes alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles.
entries.content:
By Paul Wiseman

U.S.-Canada relations, already tense, are likely to deteriorate further after the United States went ahead early Tuesday with a decision to ban nearly $1 billion worth of Canadian imports, including alcoholic beverages, dairy products and motorcycles.

The ban amounts to barely a ripple in $880 billion worth of annual two-way trade between the two northern neighbors. But it marks another ratcheting up of President Donald Trump’s second-term trade war with America’s longtime ally and trading partner.

The import ban “certainly won't do anything to help the trade tensions between the United States and Canada,'' said trade attorney Patrick Childress, a partner at Holland & Knight and a former U.S. trade official.

The latest sparring began over the summer when Trump reached back to a Great Depression law to impose 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian imports, charging that Canada discriminates against U.S. dairy, auto and alcoholic beverage producers. Canada promptly counterpunched with tariffs of 15%, 25% or 50%, matching U.S. imports dollar for dollar.

To punish Canada for retaliating against his tariffs, Trump decided to ban a list of Canadian products, effective 12:01 a.m. Eastern time Tuesday.

The Economic Impact Likely to Be Modest

The economic impact is likely to be minimal. Childress noted that the products on the banned list were already facing Trump’s tariffs. ”For a lot of these goods, the 50% was already acting as a de facto ban by making importation from Canada into the United States uneconomical,″ he said.

Jacob Jensen, director of trade policy at the center-right American Action Forum think tank, calculates that the ban would cover $967 million worth of Canadian imports, based on 2025 numbers. Of that, 87% would be alcoholic beverages that the U.S. targeted because of some Canadian provinces responding to Trump’s provocations by banning U.S. booze from store shelves.

Also banned are some dairy products — including the milk byproduct whey. The two countries have long clashed over Canada’s attempts to protect its dairy industry from foreign competition by imposing hefty tariffs once dairy imports have exceeded a quota.

The ban also covers motorcycles. Bombardier Recreational Products (BRP) in Quebec confirmed that its three-wheel Can-Am Spyder and Canyon motorcycles “will be excluded from importation into the U.S.’’ But BRP said the impact likely won’t be felt until next year because it has completed most production and shipments for the current season.

“This marks yet another escalation in the trade war that may result in further retaliation on the Canadian side,” Jensen said. He expects Canadian exporters and U.S. importers “impacted by these bans will be highly motivated’’ to demand that trade officials on both sides find some way to reach a “resolution of this whole ordeal.’’

A Threat to the U.S. Goal of a Powerful North American Trade Pact

The impasse imperils efforts to renew the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, a North American trade pact Trump pressured America’s neighbors into accepting in his first term and which he once declared “the most modern, up-to-date, and balanced trade agreement in the history of our country.’’

The deal allowed most goods to cross North American borders duty free. But since returning to the White House last year, Trump has announced a series of tariffs that have clouded the future of trade in the region.

Longtime Ally Canada Moves Rapidly to Find New Trading Partners

Trump has directed most of his ire at Canada. He is openly seeking to pull Canadian manufacturing south. And he has inflamed public opinion in Canada by repeatedly suggesting that the country become America’s 51st state.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney came to power last year on a promise to stand up to Trump. In addition to retaliating against Trump tariffs — China is the only other country to do so, with very different results — Carney has sought to reduce Canada’s reliance on the United States, which last year accounted for more than 70% of Canadian exports.

“There is now a price to be paid for access to the United States market,” Carney said earlier this month. The Canadian prime minister wants to double Canada’s non-U.S. trade over the next decade.

Carney has embraced the prospect of Canada becoming the European Union’s first associate member.

And he said last week that trade negotiations with India are making “good progress” and that the two countries are aiming to conclude talks by the G20 summit in mid-December.

Carney also broke with the U.S. earlier this year, striking a deal with China to allow a limited number of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at a sharply reduced tariff in exchange for China lowering tariffs on Canadian canola.

“We take note of the coming into force of the Administration’s previously announced trade measures," said Gabriel Brunet, a spokesman for Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc. "Our first priority remains on protecting and supporting Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses from these unjustified actions. Our core focus is on what we can control: building strength at home, diversifying our partnerships abroad, and building Canada strong for all Canadians.”

Trump expressed confidence that the Canadians would cave in.

“They’re gonna come in and they’re gonna say, ‘Sir, we are sorry,’” he told reporters Monday. “They’ve treated the United States very, very badly. I think a deal will be made but it’s gonna be fair.”

Trade attorney Childress said the standoff is likely to continue for months, not weeks. The import bans and the tariffs so far “probably won’t cause enough economic upheaval to force either party back to the negotiating table,’’ he said.


AP Writer Rob Gillies in Toronto contributed to this story.

entries.title: Arcade-Game Display Mocking Trump’s Greenland Ambitions Pops Up in D.C.
entries.summary: Secret Handshake, the group behind the display, expects the installation to stay up at the National Mall for several days.
entries.content:
Three arcade-game cabinets surrounding a plaque mocking President Donald Trump’s Greenland ambitions sprang up on the National Mall on Monday morning, allowing visitors a chance to play “Operation Epic Furious: Nuuk ’Em All.”

Secret Handshake, the self-described “anonymous art collective” behind the display at the D.C. World War I Memorial, said it was motivated to create the game after the Trump administration released arcade games based on Trump political projects on the White House’s official website earlier this month.

“In them, you get to basically play out a Trump fantasy of what his presidency has been,” Secret Handshake told The Washington Sun. “So we decided to release a gonzo fever dream of one of his other fantasies — taking over Greenland.”

In “Operation Epic Furious: Nuuk ’Em All,” the player controls a small, pixelated Trump as he “battles unthinkable evils like Fully Vaccinated Children, Woke Yetis, and the happiest people on Earth, the Danish,” a Secret Handshake release said.

Throughout the game, Trump spontaneously falls asleep, challenging the player to repeatedly press a button to wake the president up.
Greenland Secret Handshake game (1480x1688, AR: 0.88)A fourth arcade-game cabinet was placed in Nuuk, Greenland’s capital, over the weekend because “if you’re going to make a game about America’s facelift for The Arctic, it seemed only fair they should get to see it first,” Secret Handshake said in a release.

Greenland’s embassy in D.C. did not respond to a request for comment before publication.

“I hope that there is humor and fun in the interactions with the characters and missions,” the group said. “We want to make a satirical take of the insanity of the political climate in this country right now.”

Secret Handshake said the game is a sequel to “Operation Epic Furious: Strait to Hell,” which it released in May after the Trump administration used video-game footage to promote the Iran war.

The satirization of the president and his efforts in foreign policy was not received well by the White House.

“These untalented ‘artists’ should stick to their ugly ‘art’ and refrain from weighing in on foreign policy — which they clearly know nothing about,” White House deputy press secretary Anna Kelly told The Sun, in a statement identical to one provided to The Washington Post about an earlier installation by the same group.

The group previously crafted and displayed a giant golden statue titled the “Iran War Participation Trophy” at the National Mall in July, with a plaque awarding Trump for his “enthusiastic involvement in the Iran war,” Time reported.

Secret Handshake told The Sun that it took about a month to make the game and exhibit, inspired by classic role-playing games, and expects them to stay up on the National Mall for the next several days and live online for “much longer.”

entries.title: Anthony Davis Is Waiting Until After the Season to Decide on the Wizards’ Future
entries.summary: Plus more takeaways from Wizards media day on Monday.
entries.content:
Anthony Davis plans to let the Wizards season play out before figuring out his contract situation with the team.

Davis spoke to reporters Monday at Wizards media day, which marked just the second time he’s done so since being traded to Washington in February. The 33-year-old has yet to play for the team after injuring his hand shortly before being traded.

In August, Davis became eligible for a four-year extension worth up to $275 million. Both the Wizards and Davis’ agent, Rich Paul, elected to postpone negotiations until after the Wizards season starts, according to ESPN, and resume talks after 20 to 25 games. Davis indicated on Monday that he won’t decide on a long-term future with the organization until next year.

“When the season is over,” Davis said. “I’m going to go through the season, and kind of do what I do at a high level, and then, when it’s over, you know, sit down and have those key conversations again with the front office.”

Davis will make $58.4 million this coming season and has a player option for next season worth $62.7 million. Should the Wizards give him the maximum his extension allows, his new deal would average roughly $69 million annually. Should he decline his player option, Davis would become an unrestricted free agent. Injuries have limited him to just 71 games the past two seasons, which could impact his market.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Shortly after he was traded, Davis said he wanted to see what the Wizards' plans were to be more competitive after three years of tanking. On Monday, Davis said the team’s signings of Deandre Ayton and Khris Middleton in addition to drafting AJ Dybantsa were indications the organization is trying to compete quickly.

“We’re trying to win,” Davis said. “Trying to change the narrative around the Wizards.”

Trae Young’s Got Jokes

Trae Young was entertaining in his session with reporters. The four-time All Star played just five games for the Wizards after being traded by the Hawks in January. Asked if last season’s injuries to his back and quadriceps caused him to change his workout process, he hinted that he may have been healthy enough to play at times, but was held out to help the team’s draft positioning.

“I’m not really changing too much up in terms of what I do in terms of taking care of my body,” Young said. “I feel like last year was one of those years. I’m actually very grateful for what happened last year because if we didn’t, we don’t necessarily have AJ Dybantsa.”

Young signed a four-year extension with the Wizards in June worth $212 million despite his short on-court stint last season. The deal raised eyebrows across the NBA, given that Young is limited defensively with his 6-foot-2 frame and his ability to impact winning has been questioned throughout his career.

Young said several factors went into his decision to stay with the organization.

“Playing against these guys as an opponent I knew what they brought to the table as far as a competitive standpoint,” Young said. “When I got here I kind of knew that. And being as embraced as I was to the city I just felt like it could be another home for me. So it was a no-brainer.”

The 28-year-old point guard praised Dybantsa’s skill set as a 19-year-old rookie, while finding a way to compliment himself. Both Young and Dybantsa led the nation in scoring in their lone years of college basketball.

“AJ averaged 25 as a freshman in college,” Young said. “There’s not very many of us.”

Dybantsa Not Feeling the Pressure

A few questions after sitting down at the podium, a reporter asked Dybantsa if he was feeling any pressure as the organization’s first No. 1 overall pick since John Wall in 2010.

“None,” Dybantsa said. “I’m good.”

Dybantsa is one of three players on the Wizards roster who has been selected No. 1 overall along with Davis and Ayton. Assistant coach Patrick Ewing was the top pick in the 1985 NBA draft, too.

All three players were quick to point out the uniqueness of Dybantsa’s situation as a top pick joining a team that isn’t expecting him to immediately be the face of the franchise.

“I feel like there’s not a lot of pressure on me because I have such a great team around me,” Dybantsa said. “A lot of No. 1 picks come into a situation where they are the guy, everything is kind of set up around them. But I have All Stars on my team that I can really get under and get some knowledge from. So I don’t have to come in and carry this huge load.”

entries.title: Trump Is Preparing to Auto-Enroll Every Child in a Trump Account
entries.summary: Few Americans have set up Trump Accounts on their own.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is preparing to automatically enroll every American child in a Trump Account before the midterm elections, aiming to increase the impact of a program that has struggled with low take-up, according to four sources familiar with discussions.

At the direction of the White House, the Treasury Department and Internal Revenue Service are preparing to use IRS data to create a Trump Account for all children, two of the sources said. 

Republicans created Trump Accounts in their sweeping tax and domestic policy bill passed last year, providing $1,000 for babies born between 2025 and the end of 2028, and a tax-advantaged investment account for all children younger than 18. But few Americans have set up their Trump Accounts, with only 5% of middle- or lower-income families enrolling as of this summer.

If successful, the effort to auto-enroll kids in Trump Accounts could reach an additional 60 million children just a few weeks before the midterm elections. But it’s unclear how much political upside the push would actually have. Trump Accounts only provide some tax advantages, and most families aren’t eligible for the $1,000 benefit. The money is not available until the child turns 18.

President Donald Trump posted a video this weekend that appeared to tease the upcoming policy change, saying "we're going to give every newborn child a financial stake in the future.”

New regulations released by the Treasury on Tuesday say that the previously proposed department rule, which is being withdrawn, "did not provide for broad automatic enrollment by the Secretary.” The new regulations say that the Treasury has "identified an administrable structure that permits broad automatic enrollment while protecting return information."

The sources spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak with the media. A Treasury spokesperson declined to comment. Some of the congressional Republicans who helped draft the provision say the original intent of the legislation was to ensure automatic enrollment.

“As the author of the Trump Accounts legislation, I drafted the bill to provide for auto-enrollment, allowing Treasury to enroll all 70 million American children under age 18,” said Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) in a statement to The Washington Sun. “I am glad to see Treasury, under the strong leadership of Secretary Bessent, working to fulfill that promise to American families.”

The Wall Street Journal first reported on the plan earlier Tuesday.

Plans to auto-enroll Americans in the Trump Accounts intensified this summer, with Treasury and IRS staff being told to move expeditiously to get the program ready, the sources said. The bank BNY and the trading app Robinhood have been enlisted to hold and invest the money in the accounts.

Few Americans have enrolled in a Trump Account in part because the financial benefits appear to be relatively meager. Trump and the congressional GOP's "One Big Beautiful Bill" was estimated to cost more than $3 trillion over a decade, but Trump Accounts comprised only $15 billion of that total because most families aren’t eligible for the money.

Some billionaires have pledged to donate large sums to Trump Accounts to seed accounts for American children. The CEO of Dell Technologies Michael Dell and his wife, Susan Dell, have pledged $6.25 billion for children born between 2016 and 2024, which translates to $250 for 25 million children, according to the Dell Foundation.

The amount available may also vary by state. The tech investor Brad Gerstner provided a donation for Trump Accounts to make some children in Indiana eligible for $250, according to the Indianapolis Business Journal.

The plan also goes against conservatives’ long-held objections to automatically enrolling Americans in government programs, which they say represents excessive government intervention.

“People should get to choose how they manage their finances and what they want for their children, so why is a Trump Account the right answer? Using the power of the government to get a Trump Account and put their hands on the scale seems crazy,” said Douglas Holtz-Eakin, who served as the director of the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office and is currently the president of American Action Forum, a conservative think tank. “I’m worried the next thing they’ll do is put $1,000 in it for everybody and it’ll cost us a fortune.”

The idea of creating investment funds for children to use when they graduate has gained bipartisan support including as a way to close the enormous racial wealth gap. Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) floated similar ideas to seed investment accounts, sometimes referred to as “baby bonds,” and California’s Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom has called the Trump Account plan "one of the best things Ted Cruz has done.”

Some on the left have questioned whether these proposals are the best way to use federal funding. Matt Bruenig, founder of the People’s Policy Project, said he would rather see government subsidies go to help families weather their most serious cash crunch — when they have young children, not when the children are grown. Though he said a $1,000 benefit could go a long way to help families manage the difficulty young adults face transitioning to the workforce.

"We have so many issues that this is not where I would put the next dollar," Bruenig said. "But whenever people become adults, they have nothing. It's almost like a graduation gift to help you move out of your parents' house and rent an apartment. $1,000 doesn’t sound like much, but maybe this is just where it starts and it grows from there.”
entries.author: Jeff Stein, Natalie Alms

entries.title: Second Senior Prosecutor Working on Trump’s ‘Grand Conspiracy’ Probe Resigns
entries.summary: Two prosecutors tasked with investigating some of Trump’s political foes have now resigned this month.
entries.content:
A second senior prosecutor has resigned from his role investigating what President Donald Trump has alleged is a multiyear conspiracy plot from former government officials to undermine his first term, adding another layer to the tumult that has already plagued the inquiry.

The departure comes after reports of growing conflicts between the Justice Department and the attorneys tasked with pursuing the probe.

Kurt Olsen — a staunch Trump ally who played a key role in Trump’s attempts to subvert the results of the 2020 election — left his post working on the so-called “grand conspiracy” investigation based in the Southern District of Florida on Monday, according to The New York Times.

In June, Olsen joined the investigation into Barack Obama and Joe Biden-era officials, including former CIA Director John Brennan and former FBI Director James Comey. Olsen did not immediately respond to a request for comment on his departure.

The DOJ did not respond to a request for comment from The Washington Sun.

“Leadership has full confidence in the great team of experienced prosecutors in the Southern District of Florida led by U.S. Attorney Quiñones,” a spokesperson for the Justice Department wrote in a statement. “The Department’s work on this investigation continues, and we are grateful to the talented team of attorneys, which continues to grow, doing the work each day.”

Olsen’s departure comes weeks after another longtime Trump ally and legal adviser, Joseph diGenova, resigned from his role leading the investigation earlier this month.

Attorney General Todd Blanche tasked diGenova with overseeing the probe in April, and CNN reported that diGenova’s decision to step down came after a particularly tense call with Blanche regarding the former top prosecutor blocking Justice Department lawyers from assisting in the investigation amid concerns about the pace of the probe.

DiGenova did not elaborate on his decision to step down, saying only that “it was an honor and a privilege to serve the president and the department,” when reached by the Sun on Sept. 10.

The prosecutors had been looking into Brennan, Comey and other individuals who were involved in investigations targeting Trump.

Brennan and Comey faced Trump’s ire for their handling of the Obama administration’s probe into the Trump campaign’s connections to Russia that came to define the 2016 presidential election and followed Trump throughout his first term. Both have been subpoenaed in the ongoing “grand conspiracy” probe.

The investigation has generated more than 130 subpoenas, according to Axios’ report in March. The large net cast by the investigators prompted speculation about a lack of evidence, with a lawyer for Former FBI Deputy Director Andrew McCabe — who was also hit with a subpoena — calling the investigation "a vendetta in search of a crime," according to CBS News.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Hawks or Hawkeyes? Senator Flubs His Jack Smith Gotcha Moment
entries.summary: The posterboard was prepared, the questions were asked, but the game was wrong.
entries.content:
Sen. Eric Schmitt leaned on his experience as a former Missouri attorney general as he laid out questions for Jack Smith at a Senate hearing Tuesday, displaying a poster of text messages and at one point telling the former special counsel to be careful of committing perjury.

Schmitt had no idea he was about to flub his gotcha moment.

The Missouri Republican mistook the names of two sports teams: the NBA’s Atlanta Hawks with the University of Iowa’s Hawkeyes. It was a slipup that fueled false accusations, an empty threat against the former special counsel and calls from another senator for Schmitt to apologize for getting it wrong.

And it overshadowed Republicans’ attempts at the Senate Judiciary Committee to grill Smith over the probe that led to criminal charges against Donald Trump, which were dropped when Trump returned to the White House.

Schmitt touted that he had obtained the Trump special counsel investigation’s internal communications and asked Smith if he attended a Hawks game in Atlanta on Feb. 3, 2024. That date lines up with a time when Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis was struggling with her own Trump case because the public had discovered her sexual affair with a subordinate prosecutor, Nathan Wade.

The senator would later accuse the prosecutors in these parallel cases of meeting secretly to coordinate. Schmitt asked if Smith went to that Hawks game, was in Atlanta that day, or met with Willis or Wade during his time as special counsel. Smith answered no to all of those.

When Smith appeared utterly bewildered at the accusation, Schmitt doubled down.

“What would you say if I had a series of text messages from your team that said you were in Atlanta at a Warrior-Hawks game on Feb. 3, 2024 — the day after Willis and Wade announced their affair?” Schmitt asked.

His staff raised a poster featuring text messages and quickly pulled it down. Smith looked confused.

“I don’t think you know that we have this stuff, so I’ll give you a second to process it so you don’t perjure yourself,” Schmitt said. “I think you’ve already perjured yourself.”

The poster prominently featured images of Willis and Wade, the State Farm Arena in downtown Atlanta, and text messages between members of Smith’s special counsel team indicating that “109 Row 1” was “reserved for Jack.”

After more questions on other topics, Schmitt concluded.

“You may think you’re a hero in this story, but let me tell you something. You’re the villain. You’ve done so much damage — as a former prosecutor, I can say this — so much damage to the faith people have in our system,” Schmitt said. “You will go down as a total dirtbag.”

It was the wrong game.

In actuality, Smith had tickets to see Caitlin Clark play during her record-breaking senior year in college before she became one of the WNBA’s most elite scorers.

And the facts lined up more neatly with reality: Smith, who resided in Maryland, had decided to attend a game between the Iowa Hawkeyes and the University of Maryland women's college basketball teams.

When Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota) realized what was going on, she was incensed.

“Perhaps you should have looked at it more carefully,” Klobuchar said to her panel colleague.

Schmitt began to complain that he was being called out over his mistake. “Are we just having, like, an open session here? I’m glad you’re trying to rehabilitate the witness but it’s not your time,” Schmitt said, insisting that he had simply presented text messages “that could have obviously been related.”

“I think that people should have their facts straight before they accuse someone of being a dirtbag — and not get the teams wrong,” Klobuchar shot back.

At the end of her questioning, Klobuchar noted that Senate staff had confirmed the Iowa-Maryland game had occurred on Feb. 3, 2024 — and it was a game to remember. Clark scored 38 points and pulled off 12 assists, leading her team to a 93-85 win over Maryland and securing the first Hawkeyes victory in College Park in 32 years.

“It must have been a pretty good game,” Klobuchar said, adding that Schmitt should have apologized for calling Smith a “dirtbag.”

After the hearing, when asked about the questioning, Schmitt told reporters: "I asked him if he was in Atlanta. He said he's in Maryland. Maybe he's telling the truth. Maybe he's not. He's lied before."

entries.title: Trump Heralds a Government AI Bot That Won't Be Fully Functional Until 2027
entries.summary: Some administration officials previously said they hoped America.gov could be a big win ahead of the midterms.
entries.content:
America.gov is live. Sort of.

Top Trump officials and leaders from major tech companies gathered in Washington, D.C., Tuesday to unveil an AI-driven government website some in the administration hope could offer Republicans a selling point ahead of the midterms.

Americans will be able to use the website as a clearinghouse to apply for a passport, enroll in Medicare and look at government jobs — eventually. Services like these won’t be functional until 2027. Until then, the website’s main feature is an AI chatbot that looks similar to those offered by Google or Anthropic.

The project, first reported by The Washington Sun, was created by several former members of DOGE, now working at the White House’s National Design Studio. Joe Gebbia, a co-founder of Airbnb and a former member of DOGE — the controversial group that worked to consolidate government data and pushed government workers out of their jobs — leads the team.

President Donald Trump called the release of the website “one of the most revolutionary product launches of all time” on Tuesday in an auditorium filled with top Cabinet officials, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Energy Secretary Chris Wright. Elon Musk, who spearheaded DOGE, and NVIDIA’s Jensen Huang are scheduled to speak later in the day.

Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were also among the top officials in attendance.

“With America.gov, the federal government no longer stands in your way, it stands only at your service,” Trump said.

Gebbia said America.gov is meant to streamline thousands of government websites, giving Americans access to a one-stop AI shop. An FAQ included on the website says that it relies on official government sources, but encourages users to double-check its answers. The website’s terms caution that the information it gives can be “incomplete” or “wrong.”

The chatbot is operating on a “couple” AI systems, Oz told reporters, citing xAI’s Grok and OpenAI.

Gebbia said the chatbot feature would be “private by design,” and would not save conversations.

“There’s a topic that unites everyone, men and women alike, young and old, across the political spectrum: Government websites are a nightmare,” Gebbia said.

Trump administration officials had previously discussed offering tax-filing services through the website, which The Sun reported earlier this month. But ultimately, that feature was left out: Trump’s executive order underpinning the website explicitly ruled out tax filing as a feature, at least for now.

Offering free tax-filing services would’ve been a major policy reversal for the Trump administration, which canceled a Biden-era program that allowed some Americans to file their taxes for free on a government website called Direct File.

The order, however, does require federal agencies to integrate their public-facing federal services with the new website.

Trump characterized the site as part of the administration’s work to “fix” the government — in this case, its “terrible” websites and long forms — and to give Americans back the time they spend navigating them by using AI, which he called “superintelligence.” The president also thanked Musk, calling him “the man who initially envisioned the transformation of government through technology and brought us the talent to get the job done.”

Edward Coristine, a former DOGE employee who goes by the nickname “Big Balls,” worked on the website and joined Trump and Cabinet members onstage when the president signed the executive order.

Some administration officials previously told The Sun that the White House hoped that an end-of-September launch would help Republicans drive home the message that the Trump administration was delivering. However, it’s unclear how much the site will resonate with Americans, given much of its functionality won’t roll out until next year.

Trump also used the launch to press for the passage of the SAVE America Act, saying “with this, nobody can any longer complain about providing proof of citizenship or voter ID,” he said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the audience that the site would “rebuild” the process of getting a passport “from the ground up,” allowing Americans to fill out the entire application, upload a photo and make a payment on the site after logging into the government’s identity proofing website, called Login.gov. America.gov isn’t currently integrated with Login.gov.

“No drugstore hostage photo,” he quipped. Rubio also revealed the design for a 2028 passport, with a larger eagle and “more gold.”

The new passports, he said, would arrive in a special white box that resembles iPhone packaging.

entries.title: Man Shot in the Back by an ICE Agent Charged With Assaulting an Officer
entries.summary: The complaint alleges Wilber Rafael Garces Perez sideswiped an officer with his drivers side car mirror.
entries.content:
By Anna Wilder and Safiyah Riddle

AUSTIN, Texas — Federal prosecutors in Texas announced on Tuesday assault charges against a Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot in the back by immigration enforcement agents on Sunday.

A federal complaint alleges Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, tried to escape Immigration and Customs Enforcement, who pulled him over after a judge issued a final removal order, according to U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas.

The complaint accuses him of sideswiping an officer with his drivers side car mirror and later attempting to strike an officer with his car.

If convicted Garces-Perez faces up to 20 years in prison.

Garces-Perez entered the U.S. in 2024 using CBP One, a program begun under President Joe Biden that allowed migrants to make appointments with U.S. authorities to be considered for asylum. President Donald Trump ended the program on his first day in office.

Garces-Perez was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit, according to Lincoln-Goldfinch. She said a judge issued a deportation order after Garces-Perez missed an immigration court hearing because the notice was sent to a former address.

entries.title: Judge Blocks Trump From Pulling Counteterrorism Funds Over His Election Demands
entries.summary: The grant conditions were the latest in a long line of actions Trump has taken to reshape how U.S. elections are run.
entries.content:
By Marc Levy

HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — A federal judge on Monday blocked the authority of President Donald Trump’s administration to withhold some federal counterterrorism funding from states that don’t meet its election administration demands.

Courts have largely rejected the administration’s previous efforts, which reflect untrue claims about widespread voting fraud and come ahead of November’s midterm elections where Democrats seek to take control of one or both chambers of Congress and check Trump’s power.

U.S. District Judge Amir Ali in Washington, D.C., wrote in a 24-page opinion that federal agencies didn't have the authority from Congress to add such conditions to the grants, and that the conditions didn't meet legal thresholds requiring them to relate to the underlying grant purpose.

Neither the Department of Homeland Security nor its subagency handling the grants, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, immediately responded to a request for comment. The grant conditions were the latest in a line of actions by Trump’s administration to shape how elections are run, a task that has long been the job of states.

The plaintiffs that sued were Columbus, Ohio; Nashville and Davidson County, Tennessee; and El Paso and Harris counties in Texas, joined by two other Texas counties, Dallas and Travis.

They declared victory and said what the Trump administration had sought was a gross abuse of power.

“The end result is exactly what we wanted,” said Tyler Chance Yarbro, the director of law for Nashville and Davidson County.

A Harris County commissioner, Lesley Briones, accused the Trump administration of using the safety and security of communities as a "bargaining chip for partisan politics."

Twenty-five state attorneys general or governors filed a similar lawsuit.

Over the summer, a FEMA antiterrorism grant announcement included a list of election-related requirements, saying that 20% of grants for states and urban areas would be withheld until they comply.

The program includes more than $1 billion for states and local and tribal governments for a variety of programs aimed at preventing terror at crowded places, online, with border security — and around elections. FEMA expects to award 56 grants.

The list of items for states includes verifying the citizenship of all registered voters and election workers.

Places that use electronic voting systems that use barcodes or QR codes to count votes would have to submit plans to switch to hand-marked paper ballots. Every jurisdiction would have to show it audits results.

In the lawsuit, the cities and counties said FEMA had no authority to impose those conditions, “not under its governing statute and not under the Constitution.”

Congress authorized FEMA to help jurisdictions protect critical infrastructure from terrorism and cyberattacks, not to decide who can vote, how ballots must be counted or how states maintain voter rolls, the cities and counties wrote.

“Never before has FEMA purported to regulate how states and counties run elections,” they said in the lawsuit.

entries.title: How the Commanders Unleashed Marcus Mariota
entries.summary: A deeper look at how Washington catered its offense to the backup quarterback’s strengths in the win over Seattle.
entries.content:
When asked last week what the main difference is between game planning for quarterbacks Jayden Daniels and Marcus Mariota, Commanders offensive coordinator David Blough said both were capable of running the same playbook.

In fact, when it came to Mariota, Blough couldn’t wait to “turn him loose” against the defending champion Seahawks.

And how did that pan out? Mariota threw for three touchdowns in Washington’s 33-31 upset win over Seattle.

We took a look at the All-22 version of the game tape to see how the Commanders unleashed the 12-year veteran — and how they might use him this Sunday in London against the Colts, if Daniels remains out.

Short and Sweet

One of Mariota’s strengths is his ability to get the ball out quickly and accurately to his receivers. That can include deep shots, of course, but the main advantage comes from chipping away at the defense as you work your way up the field.

Much like the Commanders, the Seahawks play a lot of zone defense: Their 91.2% zone rate is the highest in the NFL, according to Sharp Football Analysis. So the Commanders attacked the zone early and often.

On Washington’s first play of the game they ran a play-action fake that gave Mariota the option of tight end John Bates in the flat or running back Bill Croskey-Merritt in the middle of the field, both wide open (below). Mariota connected with Croskey-Merritt for 7 yards.
Commanders-Seahawks (1361x768, AR: 1.77)Later in the first quarter, facing a 3rd and 10 on their own 43-yard line, wide receiver Terry McLaurin ran a 5-yard out route into wide open space because Seattle’s defense left open everything underneath. Mariota set his feet and fired off to McLaurin, who turned up field for an 11-yard gain and first down.
Commanders-Seahawks 2 (1366x768, AR: 1.78)With just under nine minutes left in the fourth quarter, Washington lined up to go for it on 4th and 1 on Seattle’s 39-yard line. The Seahawks had just erased a 14-point deficit to tie the game at 24-24. A failure would have handed Seattle excellent field position with a chance to take its first lead of the game.

Mariota took the snap, stepped back, planted his feet and fired off to McLaurin on a quick slant route for a 5-yard pickup. Washington ended up getting a Drew Stevens 36-yard field goal on the drive, and three plays later Kain Medrano picked off Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold for a 50-yard touchdown return to put Washington up 33-24 late in the fourth quarter.

Mariota was 11 for 14 for 112 yards and one touchdown on plays where he got the ball out in under 2.5 seconds. His 123.8 passer rating on such plays ranked eighth out of all passers in Week 3.

But Also Some Explosives.

Mariota’s afternoon wasn’t predicated on stretching the field. His 5.9 yards per attempt was tied for sixth-lowest rate in the NFL in Week 3, and he attempted just three passes of 20 or more yards all game. But whether through scheming or veteran savviness, the offense found ways to be explosive.

On 2nd and 10 halfway through the second quarter, Blough dialed up a fake flare screen to the right for running back Rachaad White that turned into a middle tunnel screen for receiver Jaylin Lane. This left four defenders on three offensive players over where the fake screen to White had developed. Meanwhile Lane had a convoy of blockers leading the way against just Seahawks safety Drake Thomas (below). The play went for 21 yards and set up an eventual 11-yard touchdown pass to Treylon Burks.
Commanders-Seahawks 3 (1371x768, AR: 1.79)Early in the third quarter and facing a 2nd and 8 from Seattle’s 30-yard line, McLaurin was supposed to run a 12-yard curl route. But after corner Josh Jobe flubbed on his jam of McLaurin off the line, the receiver decided in real time to keep sprinting on a go route.

Mariota, who before Sunday had completed 42 passes to McLaurin since 2024, recognized and launched the ball as McLaurin ran freely. The pass was underthrown and outside, but McLaurin expertly tracked the ballfor a 20-yard score to put Washington up 24-10 early in the third quarter.

“I had a pinch route, which is kind of like a 12-yard curl, and I beat him so clean off the release,” McLaurin said after the game. “I ran the go route, and me and Marcus, have enough time spent to where I just trusted that he was going to see it, and he did, and he put the ball up where only I could get it.”

It Wasn’t All Great.

Mariota’s ability to hang three touchdowns on one of the stingiest defenses in the league was shocking. But it also wasn’t perfect. He completed just 61.3% of his passes on the day and had some bad misses.

On 3rd and 4 on the first drive, Mariota had Stefon Diggs open on a short out route but threw the ball both behind his receiver and towards the ground, leading to a punt (below).
Commanders-Seahawks 4 (1371x768, AR: 1.79)He later stared Diggs down on a short curl route, and Seahawks linebacker Uchenna Nwosu jumped the route. Luckily Nwosu dropped the ball, and a play later was the Lane tunnel screen.

But Mariota’s Key Moment Was the Play

The audacity of Blough. He hadn’t called a single running play for Mariota all game, but in the most important moment of the game, he called Mariota’s number. If the Commanders didn’t convert on 3rd and 7 with 1:36 left in the fourth quarter they risked giving the ball back to Seattle with just a two-point lead; the Seahawks had just marched 68 yards down the field in 66 seconds on the previous possession.

Blough called a zone-read option that intentionally left edge rusher DeMarcus Lawrence unblocked. Once Lawrence committed to Mariota handing the ball off to White, Mariota yanked the ball back and took off right toward open pastures (below). The 9-yard rush iced the game for the Commanders.

“Mariota is a big RPO quarterback,” Lawrence said after the game. “This game, we didn't see it until the final play of the game.
Commanders-Seahawks 6 (1376x767, AR: 1.79)

entries.title: New California Law Bans Officers From Using Gloves That Deliver Electric Shocks
entries.summary: Immigration and Customs Enforcement recently moved to provide the gloves to its officers.
entries.content:
By Sophie Austin

SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a law Tuesday banning local, state and federal law enforcement officers from using gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to people.

The ban on shock gloves will take effect next year and remain in place until 2030. It comes weeks after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement moved to equip its officers with the gloves, which are designed to gain compliance from combative individuals. Last month, the agency awarded a nearly $17 million contract to buy 6,000 pairs.

“Trump has put his political interests above the health, safety and livelihood of American families,” Newsom said in a statement. “California is taking action to strengthen transparency, accountability, and oversight around immigration enforcement in our state.”

The law is the latest example of how Democratic-led states have been pushing back against President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts since he took office last year. In California, lawmakers passed at least two dozen bills this year seeking to fortify immigrants' rights, restrict cooperation with federal immigration agents and tighten regulations on immigrant detention facilities, among other things.

Nationwide, 17 states with Democratic-led legislatures have passed a total of more than 100 pro-immigrant bills this year, according to an Associated Press analysis using the bill tracking software Plural. The most common purpose is to limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement agents.

Democratic California Assemblymember LaShae Sharp-Collins said she introduced the shock-gloves legislation to “put a pause” on law enforcement's use of the devices while the state examines their potential risks. The law requires the state's Justice Department to study their safety and report to lawmakers by 2029.

“There's a lot of unrest and a lot of uncertainty,” she said in an interview. “A lot of people are scared.”

The law will again test the state's authority to restrict federal agents amid the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. A federal judge earlier this year blocked the state's first-in-the-nation law barring federal officers from wearing face coverings, deeming it too selective because it applied to local and federal law enforcement but exempted state officers.

Lawmakers passed a new bill this year to make the ban apply to all officers. Newsom signed that legislation.

Kevin Johnson, a professor emeritus at the University of California, Davis, School of Law, said courts are likely to ultimately rule that the state cannot bar federal officers from wearing shock gloves or face coverings. The laws are well-intentioned, he said, but likely conflict with the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution, which generally sets federal law as supreme over conflicting state law.

“The state has very limited, if any, powers in dictating to the federal government how its officers are armed,” he said.

California law enforcement groups broadly opposed the ban.

Sacramento Sheriff Jim Cooper, a Democrat and former state lawmaker, said banning shock gloves “really makes no sense" because they are among the non-lethal tools officers can use if necessary.

“When the federal government does something, the state Legislature wants to ban it,” he said at a news conference. “They're making our job harder.”

Sharp-Collins said ICE's plan to use shock gloves was the catalyst for the ban. But she cited their use by other officers, including a case in which a Kentucky family alleges a man died after being tased and shocked with the gloves dozens of times while in law enforcement custody in 2024.

State Sen. Scott Wiener, a San Francisco Democrat who wrote last year's mask ban, also authored this year's measure to expand it to state officers.

“California must use every available tool to stand up for our communities under attack from ICE’s secret police terror campaign,” he said in a statement after it passed the Legislature.

___

Associated Press writer David A. Lieb contributed to this report from Jefferson City, Missouri.

entries.title: Congress’ Watchdog Arm Is Not Assured That DOGE Protected Americans’ Data
entries.summary: Several federal agencies did not answer the congressional auditor’s questions about data security.
entries.content:
The watchdog arm of Congress says it cannot find assurances that DOGE properly handled Americans’ data.

Six of the federal agencies that once harbored DOGE are not being transparent with the Government Accountability Office about the ways President Donald Trump and Elon Musk’s cost-cutting operation handled sensitive information, the watchdog said Tuesday.

“Without the ability to examine the requested information, Congress and the public lack assurance that these agencies implemented controls needed to ensure DOGE team members appropriately secured information,” GAO officials wrote in the report.

The investigation into DOGE’s security practices, titled “Congress and the Public Lack Assurance That Systems and Data Were Protected,” found just that: It’s still not clear that DOGE was careful with its immense access to government systems.

“GAO has ample statutory authority to both conduct this work and obtain the information in support of Congress. Despite this clear authority, the agencies did not respond to GAO’s requests for the information needed to fully answer the questions posed by members of Congress,” the agency wrote in a summary of its investigation. “Agencies cited various reasons for not fully responding to GAO’s requests, but their stated reasons do not alter or diminish GAO’s statutory right of access to this information.”

Last year, Musk’s government efficiency project installed its employees across federal agencies, including six investigated by GAO: the Department of Education, the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Small Business Administration, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Various DOGE employees gained access to sensitive systems, including federal student loan information, health care and insurance data, and social security information.

Both the SBA and the VA did not answer any of GAO's questions about who within the DOGE team had access to what systems or whether anyone on those teams was following security rules. NOAA also declined to answer the question about security rules.

The remaining agencies provided “partial” information. For example, at times the CFPB answered some of GAO’s questions about access for some DOGE employees, but not for all, according to the report.

“In January 2026 and April 2026, CFPB declined to provide information that we had requested, asserting, among other things, that the information was redundant of information provided to us, was unnecessary, or that providing it would unnecessarily disrupt bureau Operations,” GAO officials wrote.

Some of the other federal agencies gave different justifications for refusing to answer all of GAO’s questions. The Department of Education cited ongoing litigation, while the Securities and Exchange Commission claimed that GAO doesn’t have the statutory authority to ask for the information.

The SBA, the VA and NOAA did not give any reason for refusing to comply with GAO’s requests.

entries.title: 1.9M Montgomery and Prince George’s County Residents Are Told to Sharply Limit Water Use
entries.summary: If power to a filtration plant isn’t restored quickly, a boil water advisory may have to be issued.
entries.content:
More than 1.9 million customers across Montgomery and Prince George’s counties are being advised to use water only as absolutely necessary as the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission works to restore power to its Potomac filtration plant.

The company issued an initial advisory Tuesday morning, and said in an update just after 3 p.m. that customers should continue to conserve water. Earlier advisories indicated that water was still safe and “there is no need to boil before essential use,” but WSSC Water said it would have to issue a boil water order if the issue was not resolved soon. The plant provides water for 70% to 75% of all WSSC Water customers.

The company emphasized that residents should limit water use to prevent a boil water advisory. The restriction is meant to help preserve resources “for system storage and fire protection as Pepco crews work to restore electrical service to the plant,” WSSC Water said.

The company urged customers to take short showers, turn off faucets immediately after use and avoid unnecessary outdoor water use, flushing the toilet after every use and using washing machines and dishwashers.

Customers have flooded WSSC Water’s social media, asking what caused the outage. The utility said it is still working with Pepco to recover the plant’s operational capacity and that the conservation request will be lifted when water production is restored.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, Pepco said electrical service is available to the facility and “initial findings show the issue affecting operations is with WSSC equipment.”

entries.title: Some Judges Sound Open to Restarting Contempt Probe in El Salvador Deportation Case
entries.summary: An appeals court heard oral arguments Tuesday over Judge James Boasberg’s review of whether Trump administration officials defied his court order.
entries.content:
Some federal appeals court judges signaled Tuesday they were open to allowing a criminal contempt probe to restart into whether senior officials deliberately defied a judicial order last year on deportation flights to El Salvador.

The full U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit heard oral arguments on the contempt proceeding initiated by U.S. District Judge James Boasberg. A three-judge panel of the D.C. Circuit this year ruled that Boasberg had exceeded his authority and blocked the inquiry, but the full court is now reconsidering.

Boasberg started the contempt proceedings after administration officials went ahead with the flights despite his order to turn the planes around and keep the deportees in federal custody.

On Tuesday, several judges voiced doubts about the Trump administration’s claims that then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem was solely responsible for ordering the migrants to be transferred to El Salvador.

One said Noem may have been a “sacrificial lamb” offered up as a sort of cover for other officials. Boasberg was entitled to investigate whether other officials in her chain of command had advised her on the decision, several judges said.

“Do we just have to accept what you say?” Judge J. Michelle Childs asked government lawyer Brett Shumate. “Maybe there are other facts that the district court needs to find out about.”

At times, the questioning of Shumate grew heated. Raising her voice, Judge Patricia Millett brought up a Justice Department whistleblower’s report that Emil Bove, then a top DOJ official and now a federal judge, had suggested telling courts "fuck you” on orders blocking deportations.

“The district court has to find out what happened and who was in the room providing advice,” Millett said, adding that “others may well have been in contempt.”

Shumate pushed back on those assertions throughout the hearing, arguing that Boasberg was essentially taking on the role of a prosecutor in probing possible criminal contempt.

“The role of a judge is not to investigate a crime,” Shumate said. If judges do so, he said, “they’re no longer adjudicating a dispute.”

Shumate told the appeals court that referring the matter to a prosecutor would have been the appropriate course of action. He argued Boasberg had no basis to continue the probe, which he said amounted to “investigating the mental state of senior officials.”

Boasberg’s inquiry, he said, was also “unclear, unnecessary and futile” because the appeals court and Supreme Court had vacated Boasberg’s original order in the case. A final order ending the probe was necessary to prevent a “clash between branches” of government, he said.

The case arose last spring when the Trump administration rushed to send dozens of Venezuelan men to El Salvador’s notorious Terrorism Confinement Center, known as CECOT. The administration invoked the Alien Enemies Act, a seldom used wartime law, to accelerate the removals without normal due process protections.

The American Civil Liberties Union sued to block the deportations. Following late-night filings and a weekend hearing, Boasberg ordered that flights be halted and that the deportees remain in federal custody. The Trump administration transferred the men to Salvadoran authorities anyway, kicking off a legal fight that has wound through the court system over the past year and a half.

In Tuesday’s oral arguments, two of the panel’s Trump appointees, judges Neomi Rao and Justin Walker, voiced some support for the government’s position and spoke little during Shumate’s remarks.

Rao, who authored the opinion blocking Boasberg’s inquiry, said Boasberg’s attempt to probe involved questions that were “quintessential executive powers” and beyond the purview of the judiciary.

Under questioning from Rao, ACLU lawyer Lee Gelernt argued that it was “highly unlikely” that Noem “made all the decisions involved here” and said that the court shouldn’t take the government’s word that she acted alone.

Cutting the Boasberg’s inquiry short, Gelernt said, would “send a horrible message” to courts across the country. The government’s suggestion that the judge had “gone off the rails,” he said, “is a little bit gaslighting.”

entries.title: Karoline Leavitt Discloses Family Investments in Trump Media and Tesla
entries.summary: An ethics document shows the former press secretary’s family holdings contain Trump’s social media company, defense contractors, oil companies and tech giants.
entries.content:
During her time in public service, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt’s private family investments included stock in President Donald Trump’s social media company, along with shares of defense contractors, oil companies and tech giants, according to a new ethics document reviewed by The Washington Sun.

Leavitt disclosed between $1,001 and $15,000 worth of Trump Media & Technology Group stock, per the document, which reflects her financial holdings and those of her husband, Nicholas Riccio, as of Dec. 31. (Filers are only required to list the value of their assets in broad ranges.)

Leavitt also reported stock shares of similar value in defense contractors Boeing and RTX, formerly known as Raytheon; oil companies ExxonMobil and Occidental Petroleum; tech companies Advanced Micro Devices, Nvidia and Serve Robotics; financial platform Robinhood Markets; and steelmaker United States Steel.

Her federal disclosure does not specify whether she or her husband individually or jointly own the disclosed stocks. The White House said Tuesday that Leavitt’s husband owned the stocks.

Leavitt resigned from her position last month. While serving as press secretary, she frequently addressed questions about the oil, tech and defense industries and occasionally addressed specific companies, such as when she spoke in November about Nvidia’s ability to sell computer chips to China.

She also disclosed between $50,001 and $100,000 worth of stock in Tesla, the electric vehicle and solar panel company led by Elon Musk, who for part of 2025 oversaw Trump’s agency-slashing Department of Government Efficiency.

Leavitt periodically spoke of Tesla during her tenure as press secretary, including in March, when she defended the company, its stock and Trump.

“The president supports an American-made company, like Tesla, who produces a very good product for the American people, which was beloved by the American people — particularly Democrats — until Elon Musk decided to vote for Donald Trump,” Leavitt said at the time.

Federal law and regulations generally prohibit executive branch employees from “participating in an official capacity in particular matters in which [they have] a personal financial interest.” There are exceptions and exemptions, including an exemption for investments of a “de minimis” value of $15,000 or less.

“Our office regularly works with appointees to provide ethics guidance and help ensure compliance with applicable federal ethics laws and regulations,” White House counsel Will Scharf told The Sun. “In this case, we believe Karoline Leavitt complied with those requirements and have no further concerns.”

Office of Government Ethics spokesperson Patrick Shepherd declined to comment, noting that his office “is committed to transparency and citizen oversight of government” but “does not respond to questions about specific individuals.”

Leavitt also disclosed that her husband owned three real estate companies, but did not provide details about their value or how much income they generated.

Federal law requires high-ranking presidential administration members to file annual personal financial disclosures to defend against conflicts of interest and enhance public transparency. The disclosures must include financial activity for the filer, his or her spouse and any dependent children.

Leavitt, who says she is now working for Trump-controlled super PAC MAGA Inc., did not sign a formal ethics agreement detailing how she would avoid financial conflicts of interest during her time in government. While such ethics agreements are commonplace for many high-ranking presidential appointees, including Cabinet secretaries, White House staffers are generally exempt.

Trump himself has disclosed thousands of stock and bond trades made in his name this year, including 1,156 trades in July alone, according to federal records.

entries.title: Lithuania ‘Ready’ to Foot the Bill to Permanently Host U.S. Troops, Prime Minister Says
entries.summary: President Trump has previously called for allies to pay the full cost of hosting U.S. troops abroad, with extra fees tacked on.
entries.content:
Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius indicated that Lithuania is “ready to pay the bill” for a permanent installation of U.S. troops and said he would welcome an American military base for his Baltic country.

“We would definitely go for it if they're ready, and we would ensure the best possible conditions for the troops, for the base to be established in Lithuania,” Sinkevicius told Bloomberg TV on Tuesday when asked about a permanent American base.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly called for U.S. allies to pay for the costs of hosting American troops in their countries. In 2019, Trump championed a plan to collect the cost — with an additional 50% tacked on — from allied foreign countries hosting American military forces. The president also recently called for European nations to reimburse the U.S. for the “Hundreds of Billions of Dollars” given to “Ukraine and NATO, free of charge,” amid reports of dwindling munitions stockpiles due to the war in Iran.

Sinkevicius expressed his desire to have “permanent stationing” of U.S. troops in the country to John Coale, the U.S. special envoy to Belarus, while Coale was in Minsk earlier this month to help negotiate the release of political prisoners held in the country.

Sinkevicius celebrated the return of up to 1,000 U.S. troops to Lithuania, after American forces departed the Baltic nation earlier this year. The returning forces are serving in a “rotational” capacity, which is how U.S. troops are typically deployed to other Eastern European countries.

“We're happy that Trump's administration actually reacted to our wish of having American troops on the ground,” Sinkevicius said. “We're feeling safer about it.”

The White House referred The Washington Sun to the Department of Defense, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The U.S. Embassy in Lithuania also did not respond to a request for additional details.

Trump announced last week that “major progress” had been made in efforts to establish a permanent military base in bordering Poland. President Karol Nawrocki suggested calling it “Fort Trump.”

Lithuania sits on the eastern flank of the European Union and is located around 67 miles from mainland Russia. The country has positioned itself as a staunch ally to Ukraine amid its ongoing war with Russia, with the Baltic country pushing for more international military aid and penalties on Russia's economic sector.

Sinkevicius spoke with Bloomberg TV while he was in Brussels attending meetings of EU and NATO leadership. The prime minister, who assumed office in July, said he discussed defense against Russia and Belarus — Russia’s close ally that shares a border with Lithuania — when he spoke to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.

Lithuania will hold the EU’s rotating presidency for the first half of 2027, and Sinkevicius told Bloomberg that defense will be a top priority during its term, along with supporting expansion of the European Union, and “addressing and inviting new countries to join,” such as Ukraine and Moldova.

entries.title: Afternoon Sun: Schmitt Happens
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Afternoon Sun newsletter for Sept. 29, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

The Supreme Court again backed the administration’s deportation of migrants to countries where they have no ties, allowing DHS to continue the removals without advance notice.

The Trump administration is preparing to automatically enroll every American child in a Trump Account before the midterms — aiming to increase the impact of a program that has struggled with low take-up.

CBP got $20 million for a “media campaign.” Lawmakers are pointing to the apportionment as an unauthorized use of funds — claiming the administration went around Congress to pay for a set of controversial Donald Trump campaign ads.





THE ADMINISTRATION

The White House’s America.gov launch felt more like an Apple keynote, including a slide deck that made direct reference to Steve Jobs’ product announcements, The Sun’s Mara Hoplamazian and Natalie Alms report.

  • Marco Rubio revealed a new passport design, set to launch in 2028. The new documents — affixed with a larger eagle and “more gold” — would arrive in a special white box that resembles iPhone packaging.
  • And the AI-driven government website? It’s live. Sort of. 
A second senior prosecutor has resigned from his role investigating what Trump says is a multiyear conspiracy plot by former government officials to undermine his first term.

Congress’ watchdog arm says it cannot find assurances that DOGE properly handled Americans’ data.

  • The GAO also found that the administration’s recent $800 million “pocket rescission” violates Congress’ constitutional control over government spending.
Scoop: The Pentagon has obligated nearly all of the $400 million set aside for Ukraine, a senior member of the Senate defense appropriations panel confirmed today, one day before the money was set to expire.





THE HILL

GOP Sen. Eric Schmitt leaned on his experience as a former Missouri attorney general as he laid out questions for former DOJ special counsel Jack Smith at a Senate hearing — with no idea he was about to flub his gotcha moment.

Senate Republicans blocked a Democratic effort to overturn a Trump administration rule they say will make it harder for people to enroll in Affordable Care Act health insurance plans and raise costs.

Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prohibited the destruction of any national memorial honoring a U.S. president — a measure meant to protect the Kennedy Center from a full demolition — without congressional approval.

entries.title: Supreme Court Allows Trump to Continue Third-Country Deportation Push
entries.summary: The justices agreed to hear arguments over the speedy deportation policy in December.
entries.content:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday again backed the Trump administration’s removal of migrants to countries where they have no ties, allowing the Department of Homeland Security to continue the deportations without advance notice.

The justices granted President Donald Trump’s emergency request to continue the speedy deportations that have left migrants in indefinite detention in African countries and stranded in nations they have no ties to.

The court announced the ruling in a one-page order, where it also said it would decide the issue in its upcoming term. The order asked DHS and the challengers to the policy to file briefs on whether the third-country removals are lawful and other legal issues, and set oral arguments for December.

“In our second Supreme Court victory in less than a week, DHS’s third country removal policy is back in effect,” DHS General Counsel James Percival, in a post on X. “A bad day for criminal illegals and open borders activists alike.”

Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson noted they would have denied the application.

In a June 2025 decision, the court’s conservative majority also sided with the government on the issue, lifting a federal judge’s limits on the third-country removals.

Since the justices last stepped in, lower courts concluded the removals were unlawful because the administration orchestrated them without giving the immigrants sufficient notice to raise a challenge.

In the application, the government said DHS had to cancel a flight to three countries carrying 70 people with criminal convictions because of an appellate court’s decision deeming the deportations illegal.

“The unexpected springing-back of district court’s order has, this Office is informed, created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations—including the cancellation of flights—and led to added expense, potential diplomatic issues, and the inability to remove dangerous criminals,” the filing says.

Lawyers for the immigrants challenging the policy argued in a filing that the lower courts didn’t bar the removals altogether, it simply required advance notice to the migrants. Those who have been deported under the policy have said they’re not told where they’re being taken before boarding the deportation flights.

“The record shows that class members removed without meaningful notice or an opportunity to present country-specific protection claims have faced prolonged and arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual assault, disappearance, and chain refoulement to countries from which the United States had already granted them protection,” the filing says. “These harms cannot be undone.”

entries.title: Congressional Watchdog Says Trump’s ‘Pocket Rescissions’ Violate the Law
entries.summary: The GAO has the power to sue the Trump administration over the Impoundment Control Act.
entries.content:
Congress’s watchdog arm says the Trump administration’s $800 million “pocket rescission” violates Congress’ constitutional control over government spending, once again raising the stakes for any anticipated litigation.

The Government Accountability Office said Tuesday that the Trump administration’s plan to unilaterally rescind money that Congress appropriated for the 2026 fiscal year violates the Impoundment Control Act, a law passed in the aftermath of Watergate to codify Congress’ sole power of the purse.

The pocket rescission “subverts both the constitutional process for enacting federal law and Congress’s constitutional power of the purse,” Edda Emmanuelli Perez, general counsel for the GAO, wrote Tuesday in a letter to Congress and Trump administration officials.

The Trump administration told Congress on Friday that it plans to rescind about $800 million in funds for programs at Health and Human Services, Homeland Security, the Justice Department and other federal agencies. The majority of the funds — about $567 million — were intended for HHS’s Office of Refugee Resettlement.

Under a normal rescissions process, Congress has 45 days to vote on a White House rescissions package. A “pocket rescission” is when the White House sends that request to Congress at the end of the fiscal year, giving Congress no time to vote on the request before funding expires.

This is the second year the Trump administration has issued pocket rescissions. Last year’s pocket rescissions were about five times larger than this year’s.

The GAO’s warning once again raises questions around whether the watchdog agency will take any legal action against the administration. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled in August 2025 that the GAO is the only group with the power to sue the administration over violations of the Impoundment Control Act.

The GAO reached a similar conclusion last year about the first set of pocket rescissions, but did not sue the administration.

“Our GC is incredibly squeamish,” one current GAO employee told The Washington Sun.

The Trump administration dismissed the GAO’s findings.

“Not a surprise. GAO has become hyper partisan and Congress recently attempted to cut their spending because of it,” Russell Vought, the Office of Management and Budget director, posted on X about the GAO’s decision. “GAO changed its long-time opinion on this very issue from the 1970s when they specifically noted the tool was available to the president. They make their legal assessments based on whether Democrats are in the White House.”

“We are just using the system CONGRESS established and never changed despite being told by your own GAO to change it,” Mark Paoletta, the general counsel for OMB, wrote on X. 

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) told reporters Monday that she’s exploring whether it is possible to add new language to future appropriations bills that would prohibit pocket rescissions.

entries.title: Senate Democrats Force an Uncomfortable Vote on Health Care Costs
entries.summary: Republicans blocked the measure, which would have terminated Trump administration changes to the ACA marketplace.
entries.content:
Senate Republicans blocked a Democratic effort on Tuesday to overturn a Trump administration rule they say will make it harder for people to enroll in Affordable Care Act health insurance plans and raise costs for existing participants.

Democrats forced a vote to undo the regulation under the Congressional Review Act, which failed 48-50, with Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) joining with Democrats to support the measure. Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisconsin), who introduced the measure, said the rule will price 2 million Americans out of their health care coverage.

“Americans have been clear that they need lower health care costs. And what does President Trump do to respond? He pushes a policy that will cause out-of-pocket costs to skyrocket, reduce the benefits you get for the same plan, and terminate coverage for two million Americans,” Baldwin said in a statement ahead of the vote.

The ACA rule change, finalized by the Trump administration in May, was touted as a way to combat enrollment fraud, lower health care premiums and offer a wider range of plans for insurers.

It implements tighter income verification requirements and new eligibility checks for ACA enrollees while establishing new health care plans, some with higher out-of-pocket cost limits and others without dedicated networks of doctors and hospitals. Democrats deride such plans as “junk insurance.”

Republicans have argued that falling enrollment in ACA marketplace plans under the Trump administration is a positive sign. The right-leaning Paragon Health Institute, for example, said that a decline in the number of those enrolled in the ACA exchanges largely represents a removal of “improper enrollees" and "enrollees who never used their coverage."

Democrats have slammed the rule for its potential to increase the costs of existing plans by luring away healthier enrollees, to reduce benefits for certain treatments like substance disorder programs and hearing aids, and to narrow the number of providers available to some enrollees.

Tuesday’s vote represents an effort by Democrats to spotlight rising health care costs and tackle voters’ larger affordability concerns ahead of the November midterms. Democrats have repeatedly spotlighted the rising cost of health care this Congress, blocking government funding for 47 days last year over the enhanced ACA marketplace premiums that expired Jan. 1.

The move also comes as Senate Republicans prepare to force Democrats to take a number of difficult votes on the cost of living later this week, including on measures designed to curb the costs associated with data centers and artificial intelligence and another to put new limits on stock trading for members of Congress.

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon), the ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, which oversees the Affordable Care Act, told The Washington Sun it’s important for Democrats to spotlight Republicans’ “hostility” toward implementing measures to lower health care costs ahead of November.

“We know that everything this administration is trying to do is to gut people's opportunity to get quality, affordable healthcare. Senator Baldwin's trying to stop it,” Wyden said. “The more you can show what the hostility to quality, affordable healthcare is, the more it tells people what this election is all about.

No Republicans spoke against the measure in brief debate before the vote.
