entries.title: Trump to Grant a Last-Minute Reprieve on Qatar Housing for Afghan Allies
entries.summary: The camp for about 1,000 Afghans who helped the U.S. war effort was set to close this week.
entries.content:
By Matthew Lee and Farnoush Amiri

President Donald Trump's administration is set to issue a last-minute reprieve Tuesday over the planned closure of a camp in Qatar that houses more than 1,000 Afghans who assisted America’s war effort or are the relatives of U.S. service members.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected to sign off on a diplomatic note to Qatar extending for nine months the life of Camp As Sayliyah, which had been due to close Wednesday at the end of the U.S. budget year, according to two U.S. officials familiar with the matter. The officials spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity to offer details before the public announcement.

The decision comes months after Rubio told Congress that the U.S. was still in discussions with several third-party countries to take the 1,039 Afghans who worked as interpreters or in other roles helping the American war effort as well as relatives of U.S. service members who have been stranded in Qatar for more than a year.

Rubio's testimony in June came after the AP and other outlets reported that war-torn Congo was among the countries where the Trump administration was considering resettlement.

The State Department would not immediately comment on Rubio's extension for the camp but said it “continues to work toward a positive resolution that provides safety for these remaining people to start a new life outside of Afghanistan while upholding the safety and security of the American people.”

The department also repeated its position that the camp is a legacy of an attempt by President Joe Biden's administration "to move as many Afghans to America as possible without properly vetting them" — an assertion that has been denied by former officials and refugee advocates.

The group of Afghans in Camp As Sayliyah includes those who fought or worked alongside the U.S. military between 2001 and 2021, with more than 70% of the camp's residents being women and children, according to statistics from #AfghanEvac. The group has spent the last five years advocating for Washington to make good on its promise to resettle those whose service has put them at risk since the chaotic U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan and the Taliban's reassertion of control.

“This is a victory for those people, and they’re going to have some semblance of knowing that they’re safe there because they’ve been worried that at any moment somebody’s going to come and rip them out of there,” Shawn VanDiver, a Navy veteran who heads #AfghanEvac, told the AP.

But he added that there needs to be a permanent solution to this yearslong crisis.

Despite the camp's reprieve, which prevents those housed there from possible forcible removal to Afghanistan, residents have little hope of being allowed to enter the United States.

Upon entering his second term, Trump, a Republican, paused his Democratic predecessor’s Afghan resettlement program as part of a series of executive orders cracking down on immigration, including dramatically altering refugee admissions to focus on white South Africans. Only five Afghans have been admitted to the U.S. since October 2025, #AfghanEvac says.

The refugee changes left thousands of people who fled war and persecution — and had gone through a sometimes yearslong vetting process to start new lives in America — stranded at places worldwide, including the base in Qatar.

Advocates have warned that if there is no alternative, the only other option for the group of residents would be to go back to Afghanistan, where they face likely reprisal from the Taliban.

In the coming nine months, the State Department said it would “continue to work to identify options for voluntary resettlement of all Camp As-Sayliyah residents.” It gave no additional details.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: Lafayette Square Partially Reopens in Front of White House
entries.summary: Fencing started to be moved back this week as officials work to make it more open to the public while balancing security needs.
entries.content:
Crews began moving back the fences surrounding Lafayette Square this week, allowing the public farther into the park in front of the White House than it has been able to get for eight months.

Visitors began noting Monday that they could now access as far as the fountains near the Andrew Jackson statue in the middle of the square. Before, the fences extended to the sidewalk adjacent to H Street Northwest, the square’s northern boundary.

A White House official confirmed to The Washington Sun that the fence was being moved back ahead of the expiration of a U.S. Secret Service request to close the park. The National Park Service initially closed the park and surrounding areas to the public for renovations in January. It was originally supposed to reopen May 31, but the fence has remained through the summer.

The official said the Secret Service “is working to make the park more accessible to the public while balancing the president’s security needs.”

The latest closure letter for the park is a request from the Secret Service to keep the area closed through Wednesday to “ensure the security of the White House Complex, including to protect the President of the United States and other government officials.”

The White House official said a new closure letter to the National Park Service, indicating a larger portion of the park will be open to the public, should be posted in the coming days.

The Park Service did not respond to a request for comment.

The fence’s movement comes after the Secret Service, in coordination with the White House and Interior Department, proposed a plan in July to permanently place an 8- to 9-foot-tall fence around Lafayette Square to “enhance long-term safety,” The Washington Post reported.

entries.title: CBP Got $20 Million for a ‘Media Campaign.’ Lawmakers Say It Was a Misuse of Funds.
entries.summary: The administration started running Trump-focused national ads that have come under ethical scrutiny for using taxpayer funds.
entries.content:
On Sept. 19, the White House Office of Management and Budget gave Customs and Border Protection $20 million for “OBBBA commemorative events.” The next day, CBP awarded the advertising company LMD Agency Inc. a contract for $20 million for a “national media campaign.”

Three days later, the administration began running pro-Trump national ads featuring the president railing against communism and praising his past achievements. The advertisements, which closely resemble past ads run for Donald Trump’s presidential campaign, have come under intense scrutiny for using taxpayer funds.

Lawmakers are now pointing to the $20 million apportionment as an unauthorized use of funds, claiming the administration went around Congress to pay for an ad campaign that the law had deemed prohibited.

“It came from the ‘One Big Beautiful Bill.’ It was taken out of funding that was supposed to be for Customs and Border Protection,” Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) told The Washington Sun. “We already have in the appropriations bill a funding restriction that is in the (Financial Services and General Government) bill, and that would have prohibited that. That’s why the administration went around the appropriations process and used an account that was part of the reconciliation bill.”

The pro-Trump ads are being paid for with money from CBP, according to two sources familiar with the spending. The Wall Street Journal first reported that the advertising spending came from CBP. 

LMD Agency did not respond to a request for comment. The White House did not confirm or deny the purpose of the contract, but defended the advertisements as public service announcements.

“These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad,” a White House spokesperson said. “The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country.”

Democrats condemned the spending Tuesday as an improper use of funds.

“It appears DHS has dedicated $20 million to this outrageous scheme, tapping funds provided to U.S. Customs and Border Protection in Republicans’ ‘One Big Beautiful Bill Act’ for commemorative events relating to border security,” Sen. Patty Murray (D-Washington), the ranking member on the Senate Appropriations Committee, and Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut), the ranking member on the Department of Homeland Security appropriations subcommittee, said in a letter Tuesday to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

“The Trump administration used funding allocated for Customs and Border Protection (CBP) in Republicans’ ‘One Big Beautiful Bill’ to pay for President Trump’s government funded political ads that started running last week,” the office of House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro (D-Connecticut) said in a press release.

On Sept. 23, the first ad, which featured a montage of Trump speaking about the risks of “communism, socialism and Marxism” to the soundtrack of “Love Me,” began running on Fox News and Newsmax. The commercial ends with the tagline: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”

The administration has now run three different taxpayer-funded ads with the same “Paid for by the U.S. Government” label. The second ad featured clips from Trump’s speech at Mount Rushmore for the country’s 250th birthday celebration, while the third reused a 2024 campaign video.

LMD Agency received the $20 million contract from the CBP’s public affairs office as part of a larger contracting vehicle the ad agency already has with the US Coast Guard.

That larger contracting vehicle is normally used for Coast Guard recruitment campaigns, according to a review of federal spending databases. Because LMD Agency already had a larger “indefinite delivery vehicle” contract, CBP did not have to run a separate solicitation process to award the contract.

The ads have drawn significant rebuke from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota), who called them “a great message” that “shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars.”

Federal law prohibits the use of taxpayer dollars for “for publicity or propaganda.”

“The ads closely mirror campaign ads aired by the Trump campaign in 2024, and the transparently partisan nature of the ads raises important questions about if the administration unlawfully used public funds to pay for the updated ads,” said a spokesperson for the nonprofit legal advocacy organization Democracy Forward in a statement. 

“This is a banana republic in which the president is just blatantly stealing taxpayer money to run political ads,” Murphy told The Sun. “There was no notification of Congress.”
entries.author: Anna Kramer

entries.title: Lawmaker Says the Pentagon Has Obligated Ukraine Aid Just Ahead of Its Expiration Date
entries.summary: Defense officials informed Sen. Chris Coons that 99.8% of the funding has been committed before the fiscal year ends.
entries.content:
The Pentagon has obligated nearly all of the $400 million in aid Congress provided for Ukraine, a senior member of the Senate defense appropriations panel confirmed Tuesday, one day before the money was set to expire.

Sen. Chris Coons (D-Delaware) told The Washington Sun that Pentagon officials informed him Tuesday morning that 99.8% of the funding had been obligated.

The confirmation caps the Pentagon’s late push to commit the money before the fiscal year ends on Wednesday. None of it had been obligated as of late July. By last week, Reuters reported, the department had obligated $307 million and planned to commit the remaining $93 million before the Sept. 30 deadline.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Coons sharply criticized the Defense Department for waiting until the final hours of the fiscal year.

“The fact that they are finally doing it, like on the last possible day, tells you everything you need to know about that relationship,” he added. “They don’t brief us on time. They don’t follow the law, and the partnership is struggling.”

Lawmakers from both parties had pressed the Pentagon for months to act.

At an April 30 Senate Armed Services Committee hearing, Pentagon Comptroller Jules Hurst said the funding had recently been released and would be “put to work very shortly.”

The department then missed a May 15 deadline it had given Congress for providing a spending plan.

Sens. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) and Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) responded by leading abipartisan letter demanding that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth obligate the money. Sens. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota) and Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina), Michael Bennet (D-Colorado) and Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nevada) also signed it.

The Pentagon’s plan included $200 million for weapons, ammunition and explosives, $99.9 million for vehicles, spare parts and equipment, and $100 million for services such as transporting military equipment, Reuters reported in July.

More recent contracts include offensive weapons and spare parts for armored vehicles but no Patriot interceptors.

Patriots are the only system in Ukraine’s arsenal that can reliably intercept Russian ballistic missiles, and Kyiv has repeatedly asked for more. Trump recently said that he will grant Ukraine a license to produce the interceptors, but the production is expected to take more than a year and would not address the immediate shortage.   

Coons said the Pentagon provided lawmakers with some information about how the money would be used, but had not yet reviewed it.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi, Joe Gould

entries.title: Appeals Court Rejects Trump Effort to Stay Sanctions in IRS Lawsuit
entries.summary: Three appellate judges sided with a lower court’s finding that the president colluded with the IRS and the Treasury Department.
entries.content:
A federal appeals court refused to reverse a federal judge’s decision to punish President Donald Trump and his lawyers for engaging in “bad faith” conduct and collusion in the president’s lawsuit, and subsequent out-of-court agreement, over an IRS contractor leaking his tax returns.

The three-judge panel of the 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found Trump and his lawyers were not likely to overturn the collusion finding. The panel left the lower court’s penalties in place as the case proceeds and will reconvene for a final decision at a future date.

“The appellants did not submit or offer any evidence to explain their litigation conduct or demonstrate that the lawsuit and the settlement were not collusive,” the panel wrote.

Tuesday’s ruling stems from a January case in which Trump and his two sons sought compensation from the IRS and Treasury Department over leaked tax details pertaining to their family enterprise.

As president, Trump had direct oversight of the same agencies he was suing, meaning he effectively ran both sides of the courtroom.

U.S. District Judge Kathleen Williams ruled that, before even filing their claim, Trump and his lawyers had colluded with the IRS defendants to eventually arrive at a settlement establishing a $1.78 billion “anti-weaponization” fund paid for by taxpayers to compensate people who felt targeted over political beliefs or actions.

The deal also gave Trump and his family lifetime immunity from tax audits. Attorney General Todd Blanche has declared that the fund portion of the deal is now dead.

“The facts before this Court demonstrate there was never adverseness between the parties; there was never a case or controversy; and there was never a question as to who would prevail,” Williams wrote in her May decision.

“The Court expressly finds that Plaintiffs acted in bad faith,” she wrote.

Williams punished Trump's lawyers by ordering his personal attorney to appear before disciplinary boards and forbidding Trump from benefiting from the settlement terms in the future.

Trump’s lawyers argued that the punishment lacked legal justification and violated the First Amendment, claims the appeals court rejected Tuesday.

“The appellants mount two main attacks on the district court’s speech-related sanction,” the appeals court wrote in its decision. “We conclude that the appellants have not made a strong showing that they will succeed on either of these grounds.”

Representatives of a bipartisan coalition of 35 former federal judges, who asked Williams to reopen the case, applauded Tuesday’s ruling.

“As we said from the beginning, Trump’s $10 billion lawsuit against the IRS was a sham, and the slush fund and global release deals that flowed from it were too,” they said. “The Eleventh Circuit saw this collusive scheme for exactly what it is and refused to stay the consequences.”
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: Hegseth Bars Civilian Faculty Tenure at Military Academies
entries.summary: The defense secretary's memo says the change is aimed at refocusing the military on warfighting.
entries.content:
By Annie Ma And Konstantin Toropin

The Defense Department will no longer appoint civilians as tenured college faculty at the United States' military service academies, according to a memo signed Tuesday by Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The memo describes the decision to stop granting tenure to civilian faculty as part of an effort to refocus the military academies on warfighting.

“To ensure our educational institutions remain firmly focused on this warfighting mission, we must address the structural mechanisms that have allowed civilian academic norms to dilute our focus on lethality,” the memo said.

The tenure designation generally comes with a career-long academic appointment at a college. Advocates say the job security is a crucial component of academic freedom. Hegseth's directive apparently would not remove the designation from faculty members who are currently tenured.

The U.S. Military Academy at West Point, the U.S. Naval Academy, and the U.S. Air Force Academy all did not immediately respond to questions, and officials at the Pentagon did not offer further details on the plan when reached for comment.

The percentage of faculty who are civilians varies by military academy. It is highest at the United States Naval Academy, where roughly half of the 600 faculty members are civilians. The academies hire civilian faculty to offer expertise in topics and disciplines that military officers don't study as part of their careers, such as English and the humanities.

Hegseth’s decision follows broader conservative attacks on tenured faculty appointments in higher education. Those efforts to rein in tenure are often presented as bids to rein in academics with liberal views.

Civilian faculty members often have more teaching experience and credentials than their military counterparts at the service academies, said Eric Merriam, a legal studies and political science professor at the University of Central Florida and a former professor at the Air Force Academy.

The academies have long served a dual role — training the next generation of officers, while providing a traditional, prestigious, four-year college experience, Merriam said. The schools offer a broad, liberal arts education, in recognition that senior leadership must be critical thinkers who can understand different points of view.

Hegseth's actions signal a shift toward a narrower focus, Merriam said.

“It does seem to me as though it’s a retrenchment,” he said. “It's a retreat from what I think was positive progress in ensuring that these elite educational academies actually have elite education as part of the program.”

In Hegseth's memo Tuesday, tenure was described as a factor that contributed to “academic stagnation, faculty complacency, and institutional inability to adapt to emerging needs. Additionally, it contributes to curriculum that drifts from the mission of educating our warfighters to the research priorities of the tenured academics.”

Traditionally, tenured professors can be terminated only under extreme circumstances, such as professional misconduct or a financial emergency. Advocates say it's especially important to maintain tenure as controversy grows over scholarly discussions about history, race, gender and sexuality.

The decision Tuesday is part of a broader push from Hegseth to remake the military's education apparatus. Earlier this year, the Pentagon severed longstanding ties with prestigious universities that had been a pipeline for military leadership, forging new relationships with Christian schools and public universities.

The Pentagon has also attempted to reorient the K-12 schools it operates for military families. It introduced a course centered on Western civilization and Christianity, part of an effort to redirect the education system toward patriotic values and classical learning.
entries.author: The Associated Press

entries.title: A Biological Age Test and Russell Brand: How Trump Officials Spent a Day With MAHA
entries.summary: Many media outlets were denied entry. But Russell Brand was there. And Bryan Johnson was leading biological age tests.
entries.content:
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his entourage of staffers and security walked through the Waldorf Astoria’s opulent lobby just after noon, even though he wasn’t slated to speak at the Make America Healthy Again summit until 5 p.m (with Vice President JD Vance).

Senior Kennedy adviser Calley Means arrived midmorning, telling other attendees as he strode through the Astoria’s courtyard that he planned to “hang out” all day. Kyle Diamantas, acting commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration, arrived around the same time. Both were slated to speak on a midafternoon panel entitled “Modernizing MAHA regulation.”

It’s common for busy government officials to pop into a D.C. event, give their speech, and quickly leave. That wasn’t the case at Tuesday’s MAHA summit, where senior Trump administration officials mingled for hours with health and wellness industry officials and MAHA activists who are concerned over vaccines, processed food and chronic illness.

The summit was the second major Washington gathering organized by allies of Kennedy where industry leaders and wellness activists sponsoring the event chatted with federal government officials and MAHA activists amid spreads of fruits, vegetables and sparkling water. The event’s organizers denied media credentials to many major organizations, including The Washington Sun and The New York Times.

Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, spoke on a panel sponsored by podcaster and comedian Russell Brand, who goes to trial in London next week on charges of rape and sexual assault.

Bryan Johnson, known for his effort to push the limits of the human lifespan, spoke on a panel about longevity. He had the audience stand up to do a “biological age test” where they closed their eyes and tested how long they could stand on one foot.

“This is an all-of-government answer to a crisis that is the defining crisis of our generation,” said Tony Lyons, head of MAHA Action, the group that organized the summit. “These numbers of chronic disease — they don’t exist anywhere else in the world.”

Panels throughout the day focused on some pet topics for MAHA and wellness influencers — exercise, disease prevention and early cancer detection — and also on broader topics like health care affordability and AI.

But elements of the programming raised points of tension within the movement that have defined MAHA’s political rise.

Some MAHA activists had criticized organizers for including insurance industry executives in the event. Stefanie Spear, counselor to Kennedy, moderated a panel about food with the executives of Walmart, Steak ‘n Shake and Sweetgreen. Leaders of major health insurers UnitedHealthcare and AHIP, the insurer association, participated in a panel about affordability.

“I think it’s a little bit of a challenge that the presentations on the stage seemed to be about bureaucracy being big business,” said Kate Johnson, a Florida nurse and mom of four who attended the White House event last year announcing its MAHA report. “That’s not the core of what the MAHA movement is.”

MAHA activists remain largely devoted to Kennedy, who assured anti-vaccine activists earlier this month that the administration is their ally. But they have mixed feelings about the Trump administration’s attentiveness to their issues.

They were frustrated by Trump’s executive order earlier this year to expand production of glyphosate, a common pesticide that has mobilized environmentalists for years — a rift that culminated in an unfavorable ruling for MAHA from the Supreme Court.

But on Tuesday, Trump officials and the MAHA world all appeared in good company. Secret Service agents swarmed the premises throughout the day.

The ballroom where the panels took place was mostly full late afternoon during a discussion led by former heavyweight boxer Mike Tyson. Organizers handed out swag bags including pea protein packets by RollinsGreens and a hand strengthener made by Gameday Men’s Health.

Patrick Kennedy, cousin to Robert Kennedy, spent several hours at the summit. He said he was there to advocate for his pet issue, mental health care.

“I mean, everyone is here,” Patrick Kennedy said.
entries.author: Paige Winfield Cunningham

entries.title: Trump Says the AI Industry Will ‘Self-Police’ Under a New Accord
entries.summary: The “morally binding” agreement seeks to help U.S. companies outpace China and adversaries without government regulation.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said the United States will allow tech companies to “self-regulate” their artificial intelligence models, after convening a group of 31 industry leaders to sign a voluntary accord to audit AI development.

"We have a very big lead, and we're going to keep our lead,” Trump told reporters outside the West Wing. “Our companies are dominating the world. They think that the federal government is doing enough, but they're dominating China. They're dominating everything. We want to keep it that way.”

The president pushed back against mounting concerns about the national security risks of AI following a recent incident that saw OpenAI agents unexpectedly access data from U.S. government websites.

Rather than pausing development and seeking federal regulations, the group of AI leaders signed what Trump called a “morally binding” accord focused on policing their own models in an effort to outpace China and other adversaries.

Meta Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg said the agreement includes commitments around building “robust internal controls and detecting if there are any issues with the technology.”

The accord — the details of which were not immediately released — essentially means companies will voluntarily implement multiple layers of internal and external audits, which will be reviewed by each enterprise’s boards of directors, Zuckerberg said.

“We want to give the American people and our customers confidence that the technology works the way we intend,” he said as Trump and other AI leaders held court with reporters.

The White House held a luncheon earlier with prominent tech figures including Elon Musk, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Palantir’s Alex Karp, Google’s Sundar Pichai and Microsoft’s Satya Nadella.

The accord coincided with OpenAI postponing the rollout of its GPT-6.1 Astra model until an extensive safety review can be conducted. Earlier this month, rogue agents accessed data from the Securities and Exchange Commission, Department of Education and Census Bureau without authorization — the second known incident of this nature in a matter of months.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told CNBC on Tuesday his company is deliberately pacing its progress in an effort to advance its safety goals.

Altman, Amodei and Musk have called on their peers to slow AI production until meaningful safeguards can be put in place to ensure such incidents don’t endanger Americans or national security. Amodei also held a one-on-one dinner with Trump on Sunday ahead of the broader summit.

Huang has said that the AI industry does not need new laws or regulations and that he believes existing legal frameworks and market forces are already sufficient to handle safety. Trump lauded the Nvidia executive Tuesday.

“We build artificial intelligence to benefit everyone,” Huang said. “We think that under President Trump's leadership, everyone is coming together to agree on how to move forward safely.”

At a state visit last week, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed to establish a communication channel for AI-related incidents, but both Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson emphasized at the luncheon Tuesday that the administration prefers limited cooperation because the U.S. holds a definitive lead.

“We cannot lose the race to China,” Johnson said. “We cannot lose America's edge because it's important for every American worker, every American family, for their safety, security, the future, the economy. But it has to be a balance.”

The result of Tuesday’s summit drew consternation from Democrats, who have called for stricter regulations on AI companies.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with the Democrats, has led the push to temporarily halt the development of advanced AI systems until Congress can advance federal safety guidelines.

“AI is planning to spend upwards of $300 million this election cycle,” he said on X Tuesday. “The result: Congress does not regulate AI. AI regulates Congress.”

entries.title: ‘Love Me’ Artist Threatens Legal Action Over Taxpayer-Funded Trump Ad
entries.summary: The artist publicly objected after the ad began airing last week, saying he “would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign.”
entries.content:
The R&B artist whose music appears in a taxpayer-funded ad promoting President Donald Trump is threatening legal action unless the White House stops using his song.

Lawyers for Christian Berishaj, who performs as JMSN, demanded that the administration pull the ad from television and the internet, saying it used his song “Love Me” without permission. They gave the White House until 5 p.m. Thursday to confirm it has stopped using the song.

The lawyers also want the administration to disclose every airing and posting of the ad and how much it spent distributing it.

“You neither requested nor received such permission,” the attorneys wrote in a cease-and-desist letter sent Monday to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

JMSN owns the copyright to both the composition and the recording, according to the letter. His lawyers said the administration did not obtain a synchronization license, a master-use license or any other authorization to use the music.

JMSN publicly objected after the ad began airing last week, saying he “would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign.”

His lawyers also argue that using the song creates the false impression that JMSN supports or is affiliated with Trump.

“He is not,” they wrote.

The attorneys said legal remedies are “under active consideration” and instructed the White House to preserve records related to the ad.

The ad featuring “Love Me” opens with Trump declaring that the United States will defeat “communism, socialism and Marxism,” as images from his presidency flash across the screen. It ends with a disclaimer saying it was “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”

The demand adds a copyright dispute to an advertising campaign already facing bipartisan criticism over the use of taxpayer money to promote Trump weeks before the midterm elections.

The watchdog group Public Citizen has also filed a complaint⁠ claiming that the ads violate federal restrictions on government employees engaging in political activity.

The White House has called the spots public service announcements and denied they are political.

At least three ads have aired nationally on broadcast, cable and streaming platforms, with more than $2.5 million spent on them over the past week, according to AdImpact, which tracks political advertising and media spending.

The administrationset aside $20 million in Customs and Border Protection funds for the broader ad campaign, drawing criticism from lawmakers who said it circumvented Congress.

Trump personally pushed the ad campaign and selected some of its footage, CNN reported. White House staff produced the ads in-house, including one adapted from a Trump campaign video.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
